title: CENDRILLON LA PETITE PENTOUFLE DE VERRE
titleEn: Cinderella, or the Little Glass Slipper
work: Histoires ou contes du temps passé
part: Cinderella, or the Little Glass Slipper
source: Charles Perrault, « CENDRILLON LA PETITE PENTOUFLE DE VERRE », dans Histoires ou contes du temps passé. Avec des Moralitez (Paris, Claude Barbin, 1697) ; texte de l’édition originale d’après la transcription de Wikisource, orthographe de 1697 conservée. Prononciation : français standard moderne ; les graphies de 1697 sont lues selon l’usage moderne.
about: Cendrillon is the tale of a gentleman’s daughter set to the meanest work of the house by her stepmother, of a godmother who is also a fairy, and of two balls, a lost glass slipper and a fitting that settles everything. Perrault places it in a well-to-do household of his own day, full of the gowns, headdresses, beauty patches and ballroom manners of the 1690s, and the notes gloss these along with the words whose sense has moved since. Of the book’s nine texts this is the only one whose transcription keeps the printer’s long s, «ſ», and the tale closes with two verse morals, the second of which wryly undercuts the first.

sentences.t: Il eſtoit une fois un gentil-homme qui épouſa en ſecondes une femme, la plus hautaine & la plus fiere qu’on eut jamais veuë.
sentences.say: Il était une fois un gentilhomme qui épousa en secondes une femme, la plus hautaine et la plus fière qu’on eut jamais vue.
sentences.l: There was one time a gentleman who married in second [nuptials] a woman, the most haughty and the most proud that one had ever seen.
sentences.i: Once upon a time there was a gentleman who took for his second wife the haughtiest and proudest woman that was ever seen.
sentences.n: «Il estoit une fois» is the storyteller’s fixed opening: «il» is the impersonal ‘it’, standing where English says ‘there’, «estoit» is the 1697 spelling of «était» ‘was’, and «une fois» is ‘one time, once’. Lectorium gives it the matching English formula, ‘once upon a time’, in every tale it opens (Cendrillon prints it «Il eſtoit», with the long s). The letter «ſ», printed all through this text, is the long s, an old form of the letter s used at the start and in the middle of a word: the same letter with the same sound, only drawn differently (it has no crossbar, which tells it from f). «épouſa» ‘married’ is the passé simple, the tense in which French tells a story: each verb in it is an event, done and finished; it has left everyday speech, and English renders it with its plain past. «en ſecondes» is short for «en secondes noces» ‘in second marriage’, and the literal line supplies the missing noun in brackets. «qu’on eut jamais veuë» ‘that one had ever seen’: after a superlative French puts the verb in the subjunctive, and «eut» stands for «eût», the imperfect subjunctive of «avoir», here helping to form a past; it is a formal tense that modern speech avoids, and English uses a plain past. «veuë» is the 1697 spelling of «vue» ‘seen’, agreeing with «femme». «fiere» is «fière» ‘proud’; «&» is the printer’s sign for «et» ‘and’; and a «gentil-homme» was a man of noble birth, not merely a courteous one.

sentences.t: Elle avoit deux filles de ſon humeur, & qui luy reſſembloient en toutes choſes.
sentences.say: Elle avait deux filles de son humeur, et qui lui ressemblaient en toutes choses.
sentences.l: She had two daughters of her temper, and who resembled her in all things.
sentences.i: She had two daughters of her own temper, who took after her in everything.
sentences.n: «avoit» is «avait» ‘had’ and «reſſembloient» is «ressemblaient» ‘resembled’: the 1697 imperfect ends in «-oit», «-oient» where modern French writes «-ait», «-aient». «humeur» is ‘temper, disposition’, not ‘humour’. «& qui» adds a second description of the daughters, which English makes without the ‘and’. «luy» is «lui» ‘(to) her’, with the 1697 y.

sentences.t: Le Mari avoit, de ſon coſté, une jeune fille, mais d’une douceur et d’une bonté ſans exemple :
sentences.say: Le Mari avait, de son côté, une jeune fille, mais d’une douceur et d’une bonté sans exemple :
sentences.l: The husband had, on his side, a young daughter, but of a gentleness and of a goodness without example:
sentences.i: The husband, for his part, had a young daughter, but one of a sweetness and goodness beyond compare;
sentences.n: «de ſon coſté» (modern «de son côté») is ‘on his side, for his part’; the 1697 s before a consonant stands where modern French has a circumflex. «fille» is both ‘girl’ and ‘daughter’. «douceur» is ‘gentleness, sweetness of nature’, and «ſans exemple» ‘without example’ is ‘unparalleled’. The printer uses both «&» and «et» for ‘and’.

sentences.t: elle tenoit cela de ſa Mere, qui eſtoit la meilleure perſonne du monde.
sentences.say: elle tenait cela de sa Mère, qui était la meilleure personne du monde.
sentences.l: she held that from her mother, who was the best person in the world.
sentences.i: this she had from her mother, who had been the best woman in the world.
sentences.n: «tenir cela de» ‘to hold that from’ is to have a trait from someone, to take after them. The mother is spoken of in the imperfect «eſtoit» ‘was’; the tale does not say she has died, but the father’s second marriage implies it, and the idiomatic line says ‘had been’. «du monde» after a superlative is ‘in the world’.

sentences.t: Les nopces ne furent pas plûtoſt faites que la Belle-mere fit éclater ſa mauvaiſe humeur :
sentences.say: Les noces ne furent pas plutôt faites que la Belle-mère fit éclater sa mauvaise humeur :
sentences.l: The nuptials were no sooner made than the stepmother made burst out her bad temper:
sentences.i: No sooner was the wedding over than the stepmother let her ill temper break out;
sentences.n: «nopces» is the 1697 spelling of «noces» ‘wedding’, a plural noun in French, hence «furent … faites». «ne … pas plûtoſt … que» is ‘no sooner … than’, and «plûtoſt» is «plus tôt» ‘sooner’. «Belle-mere» is ‘stepmother’ here (it also means ‘mother-in-law’). «fit éclater» ‘made burst out’: «faire» with an infinitive is ‘to make (something) happen’. «furent» and «fit» are passé simple.

sentences.t: elle ne put ſouffrir les bonnes qualitez de cette jeune enfant, qui rendoient ſes filles encore plus haïſſables.
sentences.say: elle ne put souffrir les bonnes qualités de cette jeune enfant, qui rendaient ses filles encore plus haïssables.
sentences.l: she could not suffer the good qualities of this young child, which rendered her daughters still more hateful.
sentences.i: she could not bear the girl’s good qualities, which made her own daughters seem all the more hateful.
sentences.n: «ſouffrir» here is ‘to put up with, bear’, a sense English ‘suffer’ keeps only in old phrases. «qualitez» is «qualités», with the 1697 ending in «-ez». The subject of «rendoient» ‘made’ (modern «rendaient») is «qualitez»: the girl’s goodness shows the daughters up. «haïſſables» is ‘hateful’, and «enfant» is feminine here because the child is a girl.

sentences.t: Elle la chargea des plus viles occupations de la Maiſon :
sentences.say: Elle la chargea des plus viles occupations de la Maison :
sentences.l: She charged her with the most vile occupations of the house:
sentences.i: She put her to the meanest work in the house:
sentences.n: «charger de» is ‘to load with, lay (a task) on’. «viles» ‘vile’ is ‘lowly, menial’, the work of servants, rather than ‘wicked’. The capital on «Maiſon» is the printer’s.

sentences.t: c’eſtoit elle qui nettoyoit la vaiſſelle et les montées, qui frottoit la chambre de Madame & celles de Meſdemoiſelles ſes filles ;
sentences.say: c’était elle qui nettoyait la vaisselle et les montées, qui frottait la chambre de Madame et celles de Mesdemoiselles ses filles ;
sentences.l: it was she who cleaned the dishes and the stairs, who rubbed the room of Madame and those of Mesdemoiselles her daughters;
sentences.i: it was she who scoured the dishes and the stairs, and polished the floors of Madame’s room and of the young ladies’ rooms;
sentences.n: «c’eſtoit elle qui» ‘it was she who’ puts the weight on her, and the imperfects «nettoyoit», «frottoit» make it her work day after day. «vaiſſelle» is the dishes; «montées» is an old word for the stairs. «frotter» ‘to rub’ is to polish a floor, waxed and rubbed by hand or with a brush. «Madame» and «Meſdemoiſelles» (the plural of «Mademoiselle», the title of an unmarried young woman of good family) are the titles the household gave its mistress and her daughters, and the narrator repeats them, perhaps with a touch of irony.

sentences.t: elle couchoit tout au haut de la maiſon, dans un grenier, ſur une méchante paillaſſe, pendant que ſes ſœurs eſtoient dans des chambres parquetées, où elles avoient des lits des plus à la mode, & des miroirs où elles ſe voyoient depuis les pieds juſqu’à la teſte ;
sentences.say: elle couchait tout au haut de la maison, dans un grenier, sur une méchante paillasse, pendant que ses sœurs étaient dans des chambres parquetées, où elles avaient des lits des plus à la mode, et des miroirs où elles se voyaient depuis les pieds jusqu’à la tête ;
sentences.l: she slept all at the top of the house, in a garret, on a wretched straw-mattress, while her sisters were in rooms parqueted, where they had beds of the most in fashion, and mirrors where they saw themselves from the feet to the head;
sentences.i: she slept at the very top of the house, in an attic, on a miserable straw pallet, while her sisters had rooms with parquet floors, beds in the latest fashion, and mirrors in which they could see themselves from head to foot;
sentences.n: «méchante», said of a thing, often meant ‘poor, worthless, wretched’ in 1697, not ‘wicked’; a «paillaſſe» is a mattress stuffed with straw. «ſes ſœurs» ‘her sisters’ are her stepsisters, a difference the French does not mark. «chambres parquetées» are rooms laid with parquet, wooden floors in patterned blocks, a mark of a fine house. «des plus à la mode» is ‘of the most fashionable (kind)’, and a mirror tall enough to show a woman from head to foot was a costly luxury. «teſte» is «tête» ‘head’, and «ſe voyoient» (modern «se voyaient») ‘saw themselves’.

sentences.t: la pauvre fille ſouffroit tout avec patience et n’oſoit s’en plaindre à ſon pere qui l’auroit grondée, parce que ſa femme le gouvernoit entierement.
sentences.say: la pauvre fille souffrait tout avec patience et n’osait s’en plaindre à son père qui l’aurait grondée, parce que sa femme le gouvernait entièrement.
sentences.l: the poor girl suffered all with patience and dared not complain of it to her father who would have scolded her, because his wife governed him entirely.
sentences.i: the poor girl bore it all patiently and did not dare complain to her father, who would only have scolded her, for his wife ruled him completely.
sentences.n: «ſouffroit» is ‘bore, put up with’ again. «n’oſoit» ‘dared not’: with «oser» French can leave out the «pas». «s’en plaindre» is ‘to complain of it’, «en» standing for her treatment. «l’auroit grondée» ‘would have scolded her’ is the conditional perfect («aurait» in modern spelling), with «grondée» agreeing with the girl. «gouvernoit» ‘governed’ is ‘ruled, managed’. «pere» and «entierement» lack the grave accents of «père» and «entièrement».

sentences.t: Lorſqu’elle avoit fait ſon ouvrage, elle s’alloit mettre au coin de la cheminée & s’aſſeoir dans les cendres, ce qui faiſoit qu’on l’appeloit communément dans le logis Cucendron ;
sentences.say: Lorsqu’elle avait fait son ouvrage, elle s’allait mettre au coin de la cheminée et s’asseoir dans les cendres, ce qui faisait qu’on l’appelait communément dans le logis Cucendron ;
sentences.l: When she had done her work, she went to put herself at the corner of the hearth and to sit in the cinders, which made it so that one called her commonly in the household Cucendron;
sentences.i: When she had finished her work she would go and sit in the chimney corner among the cinders, so that in the house she was commonly called Cucendron;
sentences.n: «elle s’alloit mettre» sets the pronoun before «alloit», the usual order in 1697, where modern French says «elle allait se mettre»; the imperfects make it what she did every day. The «coin de la cheminée» is the chimney corner, the space beside the open hearth, warm and grey with ash. «ce qui faiſoit qu’on l’appeloit» ‘which made it so that one called her’ is ‘so that she was called’. «Cucendron» is a coarser nickname, roughly ‘Cinder-bottom’, apparently built on «cul» ‘backside’ and «cendre» ‘ash’; it stays in French in both layers. «logis» is ‘house, household’.

sentences.t: la cadette, qui n’eſtoit pas ſi malhonneſte que ſon aiſnée, l’appeloit Cendrillon.
sentences.say: la cadette, qui n’était pas si malhonnête que son aînée, l’appelait Cendrillon.
sentences.l: the younger, who was not so uncivil as her elder, called her Cendrillon.
sentences.i: the younger sister, who was not as rude as the elder, called her Cinderella.
sentences.n: «Cendrillon» is ‘little cinder-girl’, from «cendre» ‘ash’, a kinder name than «Cucendron»; the literal line keeps it in French and the idiomatic line gives the familiar English form, ‘Cinderella’. «malhonneſte» (modern «malhonnête») meant ‘rude, ill-mannered’ in 1697, not ‘dishonest’: «honneſte» was ‘courteous, well-bred’. «cadette» is ‘the younger’ and «aiſnée» (modern «aînée») ‘the elder’.

sentences.t: Cependant Cendrillon, avec ſes méchans habits, ne laiſſoit pas d’eſtre cent fois plus belle que ſes ſœurs, quoy que veſtuës tres-magnifiquement.
sentences.say: Cependant Cendrillon, avec ses méchants habits, ne laissait pas d’être cent fois plus belle que ses sœurs, quoi que vêtues très-magnifiquement.
sentences.l: However Cendrillon, with her wretched clothes, did not leave off being a hundred times more beautiful than her sisters, although dressed very magnificently.
sentences.i: And yet Cinderella, in her shabby clothes, was still a hundred times more beautiful than her sisters, for all their magnificent dress.
sentences.n: «ne laiſſoit pas d’eſtre» ‘did not leave off being’ is ‘was nonetheless’: «ne pas laisser de» with an infinitive is ‘not to fail to, still to’. «méchans habits» are ‘poor clothes’, with «méchant» in its old sense again and the 1697 plural without t (modern «méchants»); «habits» are clothes in general. «quoy que» (modern «quoique») is ‘although’, and «veſtuës» (modern «vêtues») ‘dressed’ agrees with the sisters.

sentences.t: Il arriva que le fils du Roi donna un bal & qu’il en pria toutes les perſonnes de qualité :
sentences.say: Il arriva que le fils du Roi donna un bal et qu’il en pria toutes les personnes de qualité :
sentences.l: It happened that the King’s son gave a ball and that he invited to it all the persons of quality:
sentences.i: It came to pass that the King’s son gave a ball, and invited to it all the people of rank;
sentences.n: «Il arriva que» ‘it happened that’ is impersonal, like «Il eſtoit une fois», and «arriva», «donna», «pria» are passé simple. «prier» here is ‘to invite’, an older sense beside ‘to pray, to ask’, and «en» is ‘to it’, the ball. «perſonnes de qualité» are people of rank, the nobility: «de qualité» meant ‘well-born’, not ‘of good quality’. «Roi» is printed here in its modern spelling; later the tale also prints «Roy».

sentences.t: nos deux Damoiſelles en furent auſſi priées, car elles faiſoient grande figure dans le pays.
sentences.say: nos deux Damoiselles en furent aussi priées, car elles faisaient grande figure dans le pays.
sentences.l: our two young ladies were also invited to it, for they made great figure in the district.
sentences.i: our two young ladies were invited too, for they made a great figure in those parts.
sentences.n: «nos deux Damoiſelles» ‘our two young ladies’: the narrator’s «nos» is a wink at the reader. «Damoiſelle», an older form of «demoiselle», was a young woman of gentle birth. «faire grande figure» is ‘to make a great show, to live in style’, and «le pays» is ‘the district, the surrounding country’, not a nation. «en furent … priées» ‘were invited to it’ is a passive in the passé simple.

sentences.t: Les voilà bien aiſes & bien occupées à choiſir les habits & les coëffures qui leur ſeïeroient le mieux ;
sentences.say: Les voilà bien aises et bien occupées à choisir les habits et les coiffures qui leur siéraient le mieux ;
sentences.l: There they are, well glad and well busy choosing the gowns and the headdresses that would suit them the best;
sentences.i: So there they were, delighted and very busy choosing the gowns and headdresses that would become them best;
sentences.n: «Les voilà» ‘there they are’ sets the scene before the reader’s eyes in the present, as a storyteller points. «bien aiſes» is ‘very glad’. «coëffures» (modern «coiffures») are headdresses, the arrangements of hair, lace and ribbon that fashionable women wore built up high in the 1690s; the diaeresis on the «ë» is the printer’s. «ſeïeroient» is the conditional of «ſeoir» ‘to suit, become’ (modern «siéraient»).

sentences.t: nouvelle peine pour Cendrillon, car c’eſtoit elle qui repaſſoit le linge de ſes ſœurs & qui godronoit leurs manchettes :
sentences.say: nouvelle peine pour Cendrillon, car c’était elle qui repassait le linge de ses sœurs et qui godronnait leurs manchettes :
sentences.l: new trouble for Cendrillon, for it was she who ironed the linen of her sisters and who goffered their cuffs:
sentences.i: fresh trouble for Cinderella, since it was she who ironed her sisters’ linen and pleated their ruffles:
sentences.n: The clause has no verb: «nouvelle peine» ‘new trouble’ is an exclamation. «repaſſer le linge» is ‘to iron the linen’, the shifts, collars and other white things worn under and about a gown. «godronner» was to set linen or lace in rounded pleats with a hot iron, and the literal line uses the old English word for it, ‘goffer’; «manchettes» were the ruffles, often of lace, worn at the wrist. «godronoit» is printed with one n.

sentences.t: on ne parloit que de la maniere dont on s’habilleroit.
sentences.say: on ne parlait que de la manière dont on s’habillerait.
sentences.l: one spoke not but of the manner in which one would dress oneself.
sentences.i: there was no talk but of how everyone would be dressed.
sentences.n: «ne … que» is ‘not … but, only’: ‘one spoke only of’. «dont» is ‘in which’ here, and «s’habilleroit» (modern «s’habillerait») ‘would dress’ is a conditional, a future seen from the past. «maniere» lacks the grave accent of «manière».

sentences.t: Moy, dit l’aînée, je mettray mon habit de velours rouge & ma garniture d’Angleterre.
sentences.say: Moi, dit l’aînée, je mettrai mon habit de velours rouge et ma garniture d’Angleterre.
sentences.l: Me, said the elder, I will put on my gown of red velvet and my trimming of England.
sentences.i: For my part, said the elder, I shall wear my red velvet gown and my English lace trimming.
sentences.n: «Moy» (modern «moi») ‘me’ stands first for emphasis: ‘as for me’. «mettray» is «mettrai» ‘I will put on’, with the 1697 y, and «habit» is here a woman’s gown. A «garniture» was the set of trimmings on a gown; «d’Angleterre» ‘of England’ most likely means the lace sold as «point d’Angleterre», though the French does not name the material, and the idiomatic line’s ‘lace’ is an inference. The witness prints «aînée» here with a circumflex, where the tale earlier had «aiſnée».

sentences.t: Moy, dit la cadette, je n’auray que ma juppe ordinaire ; mais, en récompenſe, je mettray mon manteau à fleurs d’or, & ma barriere de diamants, qui n’eſt pas des plus indifferentes.
sentences.say: Moi, dit la cadette, je n’aurai que ma jupe ordinaire ; mais, en récompense, je mettrai mon manteau à fleurs d’or, et ma barrière de diamants, qui n’est pas des plus indifférentes.
sentences.l: Me, said the younger, I will have only my ordinary skirt; but, in compensation, I will put on my mantle with flowers of gold, and my barrier of diamonds, which is not of the most indifferent.
sentences.i: And I, said the younger, shall have only my everyday skirt; but to make up for it I shall wear my mantle flowered with gold, and my band of diamonds, which is by no means an ordinary piece.
sentences.n: «je n’auray que» ‘I will have only’ is «ne … que» again. The «juppe» (modern «jupe») was the skirt, the part of a gown seen under the open overgown. «en récompenſe» is ‘in compensation, to make up for it’, not ‘as a reward’. A woman’s «manteau» in the 1690s was not a coat but that open overgown, here patterned with gold flowers. What the «barriere de diamants» was is not certain: apparently a band or row of diamonds worn as an ornament, perhaps across the front of the bodice, and ‘band’ in the idiomatic line is a guess. «qui n’eſt pas des plus indifferentes» ‘which is not of the most indifferent (ones)’ is understatement for a very fine piece.

sentences.t: On envoya querir la bonne coëffeuſe pour dreſſer les cornettes à deux rangs, & on fit achetter des mouches de la bonne Faiſeuſe :
sentences.say: On envoya quérir la bonne coiffeuse pour dresser les cornettes à deux rangs, et on fit acheter des mouches de la bonne Faiseuse :
sentences.l: One sent to fetch the good hairdresser to set up the caps in two rows, and one had some patches bought from the good maker:
sentences.i: They sent for the best hairdresser to build up their caps in two tiers, and had beauty patches bought from the best maker;
sentences.n: «envoyer querir» is ‘to send to fetch, to send for’; «querir» is an old verb that modern French keeps only in such phrases. «la bonne coëffeuſe» is not a kindly hairdresser but ‘the right one’, the one in fashion, and «la bonne Faiſeuſe» the right maker in the same way. «cornettes» were caps or pieces of lace set on the hair; «à deux rangs» ‘in two rows’ seems to mean two tiers, but how exactly they were built up is not certain. «mouches» ‘flies’ were beauty patches, small shapes of black taffeta stuck on the face to set off a pale skin. «fit achetter» is ‘had bought’, «faire» with an infinitive, and «achetter» is the 1697 spelling of «acheter».

sentences.t: elles appellerent Cendrillon pour luy demander ſon avis, car elle avoit le goût bon.
sentences.say: elles appelèrent Cendrillon pour lui demander son avis, car elle avait le goût bon.
sentences.l: they called Cendrillon to ask her her opinion, for she had the taste good.
sentences.i: they called Cinderella in to ask her opinion, for she had good taste.
sentences.n: «appellerent» (modern «appelèrent») ‘called’ is passé simple, spelt with a double l. «avoir le goût bon» ‘to have the taste good’ is ‘to have good taste’, with the adjective set after the noun. In «luy demander ſon avis» ‘to ask her her opinion’, «luy» ‘(of) her’ is a pronoun English leaves out.

sentences.t: Cendrillon les conſeilla le mieux du monde, & s’offrit meſme à les coëffer ; ce qu’elles voulurent bien.
sentences.say: Cendrillon les conseilla le mieux du monde, et s’offrit même à les coiffer ; ce qu’elles voulurent bien.
sentences.l: Cendrillon advised them the best in the world, and even offered herself to coif them; which they were quite willing [to have].
sentences.i: Cinderella gave them the best advice in the world, and even offered to do their hair, which they were very willing to let her do.
sentences.n: «le mieux du monde» ‘the best in the world’ is ‘as well as could be’. «s’offrir à» with an infinitive is ‘to offer to’, and «meſme» is «même» ‘even’. «coëffer» (modern «coiffer») is ‘to dress (someone’s) hair’, ‘coif’ in old English. «vouloir bien» is ‘to be willing, to agree’, not ‘to want very much’; the literal line supplies ‘to have’ in brackets, which the French leaves to be understood.

sentences.t: En les coëffant, elles luy diſoient, Cendrillon, ſerois-tu bien aiſe d’aller au Bal : Helas ! Meſdamoiſelles, vous vous mocquez de moy, ce n’eſt pas là ce qu’il me faut : tu as raiſon ; on riroit bien ſi on voyoit un Cucendron aller au bal.
sentences.say: En les coiffant, elles lui disaient, Cendrillon, serais-tu bien aise d’aller au Bal : Hélas ! Mesdemoiselles, vous vous moquez de moi, ce n’est pas là ce qu’il me faut : tu as raison ; on rirait bien si on voyait un Cucendron aller au bal.
sentences.l: In coifing them, they said to her, Cendrillon, would you be well glad to go to the ball? Alas! young ladies, you are mocking me, it is not that which is fitting for me: you are right; one would laugh well if one saw a Cucendron go to the ball.
sentences.i: While she was doing their hair they said to her, Cinderella, would you like to go to the ball? Alas, young ladies, you are making fun of me; that is not for the likes of me. You are right; people would laugh indeed to see a Cucendron going to the ball.
sentences.n: «En les coëffant» ‘in doing their hair’ is the gerund: Cendrillon dresses their hair while they talk, and the imperfect «diſoient» is talk going on as she works. The sisters say «tu» to her, as to a servant, and she answers with «vous» and «Meſdamoiſelles» (spelt here with an a, an older form of «Mesdemoiselles»); all of it is ‘you’ in the English. The witness ends the question with a colon, not a question mark; the English gives it one, and Lectorium prints its witness unaltered. «vous vous mocquez de moy» (modern «vous vous moquez de moi») is ‘you are making fun of me’, and «ce n’eſt pas là ce qu’il me faut» ‘that is not what is needed for me’ is ‘that is not for one like me’. «un Cucendron», with the article, uses the nickname as a common noun, and «riroit» (modern «rirait») is ‘would laugh’.

sentences.t: Une autre que Cendrillon les auroit coëffées de travers ; mais elle eſtoit bonne, & elle les coëffa parfaitement bien.
sentences.say: Une autre que Cendrillon les aurait coiffées de travers ; mais elle était bonne, et elle les coiffa parfaitement bien.
sentences.l: Another than Cendrillon would have coifed them askew; but she was good, and she coifed them perfectly well.
sentences.i: Any other girl would have done their hair crooked; but she was good-hearted, and did it perfectly.
sentences.n: «Une autre que» ‘another (girl) than’ is ‘anyone but’. «de travers» is ‘askew, awry’, perhaps on purpose. In «les auroit coëffées» ‘would have dressed their hair’, a conditional perfect, the participle agrees with «les», the sisters, set before it. «coëffa» is passé simple: this is what she actually did.

sentences.t: Elles furent prés de deux jours ſans manger, tant elles eſtoient tranſportées de joye :
sentences.say: Elles furent près de deux jours sans manger, tant elles étaient transportées de joie :
sentences.l: They were near two days without eating, so much they were transported with joy:
sentences.i: For nearly two days they went without eating, so carried away were they with joy;
sentences.n: «prés de» is «près de» ‘nearly’, with the accent turned the other way. «furent» ‘were’, in the passé simple, takes the two days as a single stretch. «tant» at the head of a clause is ‘so much, so greatly’, giving the cause. «tranſportées de joye» (modern «joie») is ‘beside themselves with joy’.

sentences.t: on rompit plus de douze lacets à force de les ſerrer pour leur rendre la taille plus menuë, & elles eſtoient toûjours devant leur miroir.
sentences.say: on rompit plus de douze lacets à force de les serrer pour leur rendre la taille plus menue, et elles étaient toujours devant leur miroir.
sentences.l: one broke more than twelve laces by force of tightening them to make for them the waist more slender, and they were always before their mirror.
sentences.i: more than a dozen laces were broken in drawing them tight to make their waists smaller, and they were forever in front of the mirror.
sentences.n: The «lacets» are the laces of the stays, the stiffened bodice drawn tight about a woman’s waist. «à force de» with an infinitive is ‘by dint of, through so much’. In «pour leur rendre la taille plus menuë» ‘to make for them the waist more slender’, «taille» is ‘waist, figure’, and «leur» ‘to them’ does the work of English ‘their’. «menuë» is «menue» ‘slender’, and «toûjours» is «toujours» ‘always’.

sentences.t: Enfin l’heureux jour arriva ; on partit, & Cendrillon les ſuivit des yeux le plus longtemps qu’elle put ;
sentences.say: Enfin l’heureux jour arriva ; on partit, et Cendrillon les suivit des yeux le plus longtemps qu’elle put ;
sentences.l: At last the happy day arrived; one left, and Cendrillon followed them with the eyes the longest that she could;
sentences.i: At last the happy day came; they set off, and Cinderella watched them go for as long as she could;
sentences.n: Three passés simples in a row, «arriva», «partit», «ſuivit», move the story on event by event. «on partit» ‘one left’ is ‘they set off’. «ſuivre des yeux» ‘to follow with the eyes’ is ‘to watch (someone) go’, and «le plus longtemps qu’elle put» is ‘as long as she could’.

sentences.t: lorſqu’elle ne les vit plus, elle ſe mit à pleurer.
sentences.say: lorsqu’elle ne les vit plus, elle se mit à pleurer.
sentences.l: when she saw them no more, she set herself to weeping.
sentences.i: when she could see them no longer, she began to cry.
sentences.n: «ne … plus» is ‘no more, no longer’. «ſe mettre à» with an infinitive is ‘to begin to’, literally ‘to set oneself to’. «vit» is the passé simple of «voir», and «lorſqu’elle» is «lorsqu’elle» ‘when she’.

sentences.t: Sa Maraine, qui la vit toute en pleurs, luy demanda ce qu’elle avoit : Je voudrois bien… Je voudrois bien… elle pleuroit ſi fort qu’elle ne put achever :
sentences.say: Sa Marraine, qui la vit toute en pleurs, lui demanda ce qu’elle avait : Je voudrais bien… Je voudrais bien… elle pleurait si fort qu’elle ne put achever :
sentences.l: Her godmother, who saw her all in tears, asked her what she had: I would like well… I would like well… she wept so hard that she could not finish:
sentences.i: Her godmother, who found her all in tears, asked her what was the matter. I should so like… I should so like… She was crying so hard that she could not finish;
sentences.n: «Maraine» is the 1697 spelling of «marraine» ‘godmother’, with one r. «ce qu’elle avoit» ‘what she had’ is ‘what was the matter with her’. «Je voudrois bien» (modern «voudrais») ‘I would like well’ is ‘I should so much like’: «bien» warms the wish. The broken-off words run straight into the narrator’s «elle pleuroit», with no mark between, as the witness prints them.

sentences.t: ſa Maraine, qui eſtoit Fée, luy dit, tu voudrois bien aller au Bal, n’eſt-ce pas : Helas ! ouy, dit Cendrillon en ſoûpirant :
sentences.say: sa Marraine, qui était Fée, lui dit, tu voudrais bien aller au Bal, n’est-ce pas : Hélas ! oui, dit Cendrillon en soupirant :
sentences.l: her godmother, who was a fairy, said to her, you would like well to go to the ball, is it not? Alas! yes, said Cendrillon, sighing:
sentences.i: her godmother, who was a fairy, said to her, You would like to go to the ball, would you not? Alas, yes, said Cinderella with a sigh;
sentences.n: «Maraine, qui eſtoit Fée» is read as the noun, ‘who was a fairy’, since the tale goes on to call her «la Fée»; elsewhere in the book «Fée» can also be an adjective, ‘enchanted’, as of Bluebeard’s key. «n’eſt-ce pas» ‘is it not’ asks for agreement, and the witness again closes the question with a colon; the English gives it a question mark. The godmother says «tu», as to a child. «ouy» is «oui» ‘yes’, and «en ſoûpirant» (modern «en soupirant») ‘in sighing’ is ‘with a sigh’.

sentences.t: Hé bien ! ſeras-tu bonne fille ? dit ſa Maraine ; je t’y feray aller ?
sentences.say: Hé bien ! seras-tu bonne fille ? dit sa Marraine ; je t’y ferai aller ?
sentences.l: Well then! will you be a good girl? said her godmother; I will make you go there.
sentences.i: Well then, will you be a good girl? said her godmother. Then I shall see that you go.
sentences.n: «Hé bien» (modern «Eh bien») is ‘well then’, and «bonne fille» is ‘a good girl’, one who does as she is told. In «je t’y feray aller» ‘I will make you go there’, «faire» with an infinitive is ‘to make (someone) do’, «y» ‘there’ is the ball, and «feray» is «ferai». The witness ends this with a question mark, though it reads more naturally as a promise than a question; the English gives it a full stop, and Lectorium prints its witness unaltered.

sentences.t: Elle la mena dans ſa chambre, et luy dit, va dans le jardin & apporte moy une citroüille :
sentences.say: Elle la mena dans sa chambre, et lui dit, va dans le jardin et apporte moi une citrouille :
sentences.l: She led her into her room, and said to her, go into the garden and bring me a pumpkin:
sentences.i: She took her into her room and said to her, Go into the garden and bring me a pumpkin;
sentences.n: «mena» is the passé simple of «mener» ‘to lead, to take’, and «ſa chambre» is the godmother’s own room. «va» and «apporte» are «tu» imperatives. «apporte moy» is printed without the hyphen of modern «apporte-moi», and «citroüille» is «citrouille» ‘pumpkin’, with the diaeresis the printer sets on many a «u».

sentences.t: Cendrillon alla auſſi toſt cueillir la plus belle qu’elle put trouver, & la porta à ſa Maraine, ne pouvant deviner comment cette citroüille la pouroit faire aller au bal :
sentences.say: Cendrillon alla aussi tôt cueillir la plus belle qu’elle put trouver, et la porta à sa Marraine, ne pouvant deviner comment cette citrouille la pourrait faire aller au bal :
sentences.l: Cendrillon went at once to pick the most beautiful that she could find, and carried it to her godmother, not being able to guess how this pumpkin could make her go to the ball:
sentences.i: Cinderella went straight away and picked the finest she could find, and brought it to her godmother, though she could not guess how a pumpkin could get her to the ball;
sentences.n: «auſſi toſt» is «aussitôt» ‘at once’, printed here as two words and later as «auſſi-toſt». «cueillir» is ‘to pick, to gather’. «ne pouvant deviner» ‘not being able to guess’ leaves out «pas», as «pouvoir» can. In «la pouroit faire aller» ‘could make her go’ the pronoun stands before «pouroit», the 1697 order, and «pouroit» is «pourrait» printed with a single r.

sentences.t: ſa Maraine la creuſa, & n’ayant laiſſé que l’écorce, la frappa de ſa baguette, & la citroüille fut auſſi-toſt changée en un beau caroſſe tout doré.
sentences.say: sa Marraine la creusa, et n’ayant laissé que l’écorce, la frappa de sa baguette, et la citrouille fut aussitôt changée en un beau carrosse tout doré.
sentences.l: her godmother hollowed it, and having left only the rind, struck it with her wand, and the pumpkin was at once changed into a beautiful coach all gilded.
sentences.i: her godmother hollowed it out, and when nothing was left but the rind she struck it with her wand, and the pumpkin was instantly turned into a fine coach, gilded all over.
sentences.n: «creuſa» is the passé simple of «creuser» ‘to hollow out’. «n’ayant laiſſé que l’écorce» ‘having left only the rind’ is «ne … que» with a perfect participle. «baguette» is ‘wand’. A «caroſſe» (modern «carrosse») was a closed coach hung on straps or springs, the carriage of people of rank, and «tout doré» is ‘gilded all over’.

sentences.t: Enſuite, elle alla regarder dans ſa ſouriſſiere, où elle trouva ſix ſouris toutes en vie ;
sentences.say: Ensuite, elle alla regarder dans sa souricière, où elle trouva six souris toutes en vie ;
sentences.l: Next, she went to look in her mousetrap, where she found six mice all alive;
sentences.i: Then she went to look in her mousetrap, and found six mice in it, all still alive;
sentences.n: «ſouriſſiere» (modern «souricière») is a mousetrap, here one that has taken its mice alive, built on «ſouris» ‘mouse’, whose plural is the same word. «toutes en vie» is ‘all alive’, with «toutes» agreeing with the feminine «ſouris». «Enſuite» is ‘next, then’.

sentences.t: elle dit à Cendrillon de lever un peu la trappe de la ſouriſſiere, & à chaque ſouris qui ſortoit, elle luy donnoit un coup de ſa baguette, & la ſouris eſtoit auſſi-toſt changée en un beau cheval ;
sentences.say: elle dit à Cendrillon de lever un peu la trappe de la souricière, et à chaque souris qui sortait, elle lui donnait un coup de sa baguette, et la souris était aussitôt changée en un beau cheval ;
sentences.l: she told Cendrillon to lift a little the trapdoor of the mousetrap, and at each mouse that came out, she gave it a blow of her wand, and the mouse was at once changed into a beautiful horse;
sentences.i: she told Cinderella to raise the trapdoor a little, and as each mouse came out she gave it a tap with her wand, and the mouse was at once turned into a fine horse;
sentences.n: «dire à quelqu’un de» with an infinitive is ‘to tell someone to’. The imperfects «ſortoit», «donnoit», «eſtoit» repeat the magic six times over, one mouse after another. «un coup de ſa baguette» ‘a blow of her wand’ is only a light stroke, and «luy» ‘to it’ is the mouse.

sentences.t: ce qui fit un bel attelage de ſix chevaux d’un beau gris de ſouris pommelé :
sentences.say: ce qui fit un bel attelage de six chevaux d’un beau gris de souris pommelé :
sentences.l: which made a fine team of six horses of a fine mouse-grey dappled:
sentences.i: which made a fine team of six horses of a handsome dappled mouse-grey;
sentences.n: An «attelage» is a team of horses harnessed together, and six horses to a coach was a sign of great state. «gris de ſouris» ‘mouse grey’ was a real name for a horse’s coat, and «pommelé» ‘dappled’, from «pomme» ‘apple’, describes round patches in it: the mice keep their colour. «bel» is the form «beau» takes before a vowel.

sentences.t: Comme elle eſtoit en peine de quoy elle ferait un Cocher, je vais voir, dit Cendrillon, s’il n’y a point quelque rat dans la ratiere ; nous en ferons un Cocher : Tu as raiſon, dit ſa Maraine, va voir :
sentences.say: Comme elle était en peine de quoi elle ferait un Cocher, je vais voir, dit Cendrillon, s’il n’y a point quelque rat dans la ratière ; nous en ferons un Cocher : Tu as raison, dit sa Marraine, va voir :
sentences.l: As she was in difficulty [over] what she would make a coachman of, I am going to see, said Cendrillon, if there is not some rat in the rat-trap; we will make of it a coachman: You are right, said her godmother, go see:
sentences.i: As the godmother was at a loss for something to make a coachman of, I will go and see, said Cinderella, whether there isn’t a rat in the rat-trap; we can make a coachman of him. You are right, said her godmother, go and see.
sentences.n: «eſtre en peine de» is ‘to be at a loss about, troubled over’; the literal line supplies ‘over’ in brackets, and the idiomatic line names the godmother, whom the French leaves as «elle». «de quoy elle ferait un Cocher» is ‘out of what she would make a coachman’: «faire un cocher de» is ‘to make a coachman out of’, and «en» in «nous en ferons» is ‘of it’, the rat. «ferait» is printed here with the modern ending, beside the tale’s usual «-oit». «s’il n’y a point quelque rat» ‘if there isn’t some rat’ hopes for a yes. Cendrillon joins in with «nous» ‘we’, and the godmother answers with «tu».

sentences.t: Cendrillon lui apporta la ratiere, où il y avoit trois gros rats.
sentences.say: Cendrillon lui apporta la ratière, où il y avait trois gros rats.
sentences.l: Cendrillon brought her the rat-trap, where there were three big rats.
sentences.i: Cinderella brought her the rat-trap, which had three big rats in it.
sentences.n: «il y avoit» ‘there there-had’ is ‘there were’: «il y a» keeps its singular verb before a plural. «lui» is printed here in its modern spelling, where the tale mostly has «luy». «ratiere» is «ratière» ‘rat-trap’.

sentences.t: La fée en prit un d’entre les trois, à cauſe de ſa maîtreſſe barbe, & l’ayant touché, il fut changé en un gros Cocher qui avoit une des plus belles mouſtaches qu’on ait jamais veuës.
sentences.say: La fée en prit un d’entre les trois, à cause de sa maîtresse barbe, et l’ayant touché, il fut changé en un gros Cocher qui avait une des plus belles moustaches qu’on ait jamais vues.
sentences.l: The fairy took one of them from among the three, because of his master beard, and having touched him, he was changed into a fat coachman who had one of the finest moustaches that one has ever seen.
sentences.i: The fairy chose one of the three for his splendid whiskers, and once she had touched him he was turned into a stout coachman with one of the finest moustaches ever seen.
sentences.n: «maîtreſſe barbe» ‘master beard’: «maître», feminine «maîtresse», before a noun meant ‘chief, commanding, first-rate’, so these are whiskers to be proud of. In «l’ayant touché, il fut changé» ‘having touched him, he was changed’ the participle belongs to the fairy while the main clause turns to the rat, a looseness 1697 allowed. «gros» is ‘stout, big’. «qu’on ait jamais veuës» ‘that one has ever seen’ is the subjunctive after a superlative, here in the perfect, with «veuës» agreeing with «mouſtaches». The witness prints «fée» here in lower case.

sentences.t: Enſuite elle luy dit, va dans le jardin, tu y trouveras ſix lezards derriere l’arroſoir, apporte les moy, elle ne les eut pas plûtoſt apportez, que la Maraine les changea en ſix Laquais, qui monterent auſſi-toſt derriere le caroſſe avec leurs habits chamarez, & qui s’y tenoient attachez, comme s’ils n’euſſent fait autre choſe de toute leur vie.
sentences.say: Ensuite elle lui dit, va dans le jardin, tu y trouveras six lézards derrière l’arrosoir, apporte les moi, elle ne les eut pas plutôt apportés, que la Marraine les changea en six Laquais, qui montèrent aussitôt derrière le carrosse avec leurs habits chamarrés, et qui s’y tenaient attachés, comme s’ils n’eussent fait autre chose de toute leur vie.
sentences.l: Next she said to her, go into the garden, you will find there six lizards behind the watering-can, bring them to me, she had no sooner brought them, than the godmother changed them into six lackeys, who climbed at once behind the coach with their braided clothes, and who held on there, as if they had done no other thing in all their life.
sentences.i: Then she said to her, Go into the garden; behind the watering-can you will find six lizards; bring them to me. No sooner had she brought them than the godmother turned them into six footmen, who at once climbed up behind the coach in their braided liveries and clung on there as if they had never done anything else in their lives.
sentences.n: «apporte les moy» is «apporte-les-moi» ‘bring them to me’, printed without hyphens. The witness runs the order and what follows into one sentence joined by commas, and «elle ne les eut pas plûtoſt apportez, que» ‘she had no sooner brought them than’ begins a new action: «eut … apportez» is the past anterior, the passé simple of «avoir» with a participle, and «apportez» is «apportés». «Laquais» were footmen in livery, who rode standing at the back of a coach. «chamarez» (printed «chamarrez» a sentence later, modern «chamarrés») is ‘trimmed with braid or lace’. «comme s’ils n’euſſent fait autre choſe» ‘as if they had done no other thing’ has the pluperfect subjunctive, built on the imperfect subjunctive «euſſent», where modern French uses the indicative «avaient fait». «lezards» is «lézards» ‘lizards’.

sentences.t: La Fée dit alors à Cendrillon : Hé bien ? voilà de quoy aller au bal, n’eſ-tu pas bien aiſe ? Ouy, mais eſt-ce que j’irai comme cela, avec mes vilains habits :
sentences.say: La Fée dit alors à Cendrillon : Hé bien ? voilà de quoi aller au bal, n’es-tu pas bien aise ? Oui, mais est-ce que j’irai comme cela, avec mes vilains habits :
sentences.l: The fairy said then to Cendrillon: Well then? there is the wherewithal to go to the ball, are you not well glad? Yes, but is it that I shall go like that, with my ugly clothes?
sentences.i: Then the fairy said to Cinderella, Well now, here is all you need to go to the ball; are you not pleased? Yes, but am I to go like this, in these ugly clothes of mine?
sentences.n: «voilà de quoy aller au bal» ‘there is (the means) wherewith to go to the ball’: «de quoi» with an infinitive is ‘what is needed to’. «n’eſ-tu pas» is ‘are you not’, with «eſ» simply «es» ‘are’, printed with the long s. «eſt-ce que» ‘is it that’ turns a statement into a question, and «irai» ‘I shall go’ is the future of «aller». «vilains» is ‘ugly, wretched’. The question again ends on a colon in the witness, and the English gives it a question mark.

sentences.t: Sa maraine ne fit que la toucher avec ſa baguette, & en même tems ſes habits furent changez en des habits de drap d’or & d’argent, tout chamarrez de pierreries :
sentences.say: Sa marraine ne fit que la toucher avec sa baguette, et en même temps ses habits furent changés en des habits de drap d’or et d’argent, tout chamarrés de pierreries :
sentences.l: Her godmother did nothing but touch her with her wand, and at the same time her clothes were changed into clothes of cloth of gold and of silver, all bedecked with precious stones:
sentences.i: Her godmother merely touched her with her wand, and in that same moment her clothes were changed into garments of gold and silver cloth, covered all over with jewels;
sentences.n: «ne fit que» with an infinitive is ‘did nothing but, merely’. «en même tems» is ‘at the same moment’, «tems» being a spelling of «temps» without the p, common at the time. «drap d’or & d’argent» is cloth woven with threads of gold and silver, the richest of stuffs. «chamarrez de pierreries» is ‘trimmed all over with precious stones’, and «pierreries» are gems. The witness prints «maraine» here in lower case.

sentences.t: elle luy donna enſuite une paire de pentoufles de verre, les plus jolies du monde.
sentences.say: elle lui donna ensuite une paire de pantoufles de verre, les plus jolies du monde.
sentences.l: she gave her next a pair of slippers of glass, the prettiest in the world.
sentences.i: then she gave her a pair of glass slippers, the prettiest in the world.
sentences.n: Each time the book says what the slippers are made of (three times in the tale, and once in the title) it prints «verre» ‘glass’, and Lectorium translates glass. The reading «vair», a squirrel fur whose name sounds the same, is a later conjecture with no support in this edition. The book spells the word both «pantoufle» and «pentoufle» (the first mention is «pentoufles de verre», and the title has «PENTOUFLE»); they are one word, modern «pantoufle», and «la petite pentoufle» is ‘the little slipper’. «les plus jolies du monde» ‘the prettiest in the world’ agrees with the feminine plural «pentoufles».

sentences.t: Quand elle fut ainſi parée, elle monta en caroſſe ;
sentences.say: Quand elle fut ainsi parée, elle monta en carrosse ;
sentences.l: When she was thus adorned, she mounted into [the] coach;
sentences.i: When she was thus arrayed, she stepped into the coach;
sentences.n: «parée» is ‘adorned, dressed in finery’, from «ſe parer» ‘to adorn oneself’, and «fut … parée» is the passé simple of «être» with a participle. «monter en caroſſe» ‘to mount in coach’, with no article, is the set phrase for getting into a carriage; the literal line supplies ‘the’ in brackets.

sentences.t: mais ſa Maraine luy recommanda, ſur toutes choſes, de ne pas paſſer minuit, l’avertiſſant que, ſi elle demeuroit au bal un moment davantage, ſon caroſſe redeviendroit citroüille, ſes chevaux des ſourils, ſes laquais des lezards, et que ſes vieux habits reprendroient leur première forme.
sentences.say: mais sa Marraine lui recommanda, sur toutes choses, de ne pas passer minuit, l’avertissant que, si elle demeurait au bal un moment davantage, son carrosse redeviendrait citrouille, ses chevaux des souris, ses laquais des lézards, et que ses vieux habits reprendraient leur première forme.
sentences.l: but her godmother enjoined her, above all things, not to pass midnight, warning her that, if she stayed at the ball a moment more, her coach would become pumpkin again, her horses mice, her lackeys lizards, and that her old clothes would take again their first form.
sentences.i: but above all things her godmother charged her not to stay past midnight, warning her that if she remained at the ball one moment longer her coach would turn back into a pumpkin, her horses into mice, her footmen into lizards, and her old clothes would return to what they had been.
sentences.n: «recommander à quelqu’un de» with an infinitive is ‘to charge, to urge someone to’, stronger than English ‘recommend’, and «ſur toutes choſes» is ‘above all’. «demeuroit» (modern «demeurait») is ‘stayed, remained’, and the conditionals «redeviendroit», «reprendroient» give what would follow; «re-» is ‘back, again’. The witness prints «ſourils» where the tale everywhere else has «ſouris» ‘mice’; the sense is plainly ‘mice’, and Lectorium prints its witness unaltered. «reprendre leur première forme» is ‘to take back their first shape’.

sentences.t: Elle promit à ſa Maraine qu’elle ne manqueroit pas de ſortir du bal avant minuit :
sentences.say: Elle promit à sa Marraine qu’elle ne manquerait pas de sortir du bal avant minuit :
sentences.l: She promised her godmother that she would not fail to leave the ball before midnight:
sentences.i: She promised her godmother that she would be sure to leave the ball before midnight.
sentences.n: «ne pas manquer de» with an infinitive is ‘not to fail to’, and «manqueroit» is the 1697 spelling of «manquerait». «promit» is the passé simple of «promettre» ‘to promise’.

sentences.t: Elle part, ne ſe ſentant pas de joye.
sentences.say: Elle part, ne se sentant pas de joie.
sentences.l: She leaves, not feeling herself for joy.
sentences.i: Off she goes, beside herself with joy.
sentences.n: «part» ‘leaves’ is in the present tense: after a run of passés simples the story leaps into the present and sets the departure before the reader’s eyes. «ne ſe ſentir pas de joye» ‘not to feel oneself for joy’ is ‘to be beside oneself with joy’, and «joye» is «joie».

sentences.t: Le Fils du Roi, qu’on alla avertir qu’il venoit d’arriver une grande Princeſſe qu’on ne connoissoit point, courut la recevoir ;
sentences.say: Le Fils du Roi, qu’on alla avertir qu’il venait d’arriver une grande Princesse qu’on ne connaissait point, courut la recevoir ;
sentences.l: The King’s son, whom one went to inform that there had just arrived a great princess whom one did not know, ran to receive her;
sentences.i: The King’s son, on being told that a great princess whom nobody knew had just arrived, ran out to receive her;
sentences.n: «qu’on alla avertir» ‘whom one went to inform’: someone went to tell him. «il venoit d’arriver une grande Princeſſe» ‘there had just arrived a great princess’ is impersonal «il», with the princess after the verb, and «venir de» with an infinitive is ‘to have just (done)’. «qu’on ne connoiſſoit point» is ‘whom no one knew at all’; the witness prints this «connoissoit» with round s. «courut» is the passé simple of «courir» ‘to run’.

sentences.t: il luy donna la main à la deſcente du caroſſe, & la mena dans la ſalle où eſtoit la compagnie :
sentences.say: il lui donna la main à la descente du carrosse, et la mena dans la salle où était la compagnie :
sentences.l: he gave her the hand at the descent from the coach, and led her into the hall where the company was:
sentences.i: he gave her his hand as she stepped down from the coach, and led her into the hall where the company was gathered;
sentences.n: To «donner la main» to a lady was to offer her one’s hand, a courtesy that honoured her as she alighted. «la deſcente du caroſſe» ‘the descent from the coach’ is the moment of stepping down. The «ſalle» is the great hall, and «la compagnie» the assembled guests; «où eſtoit la compagnie» puts the subject after its verb, as French often does after «où».

sentences.t: il ſe fit alors un grand ſilence ; on ceſſa de danſer, & les violons ne joüerent plus, tant on eſtoit attentif à contempler les grandes beautez de cet inconnuë :
sentences.say: il se fit alors un grand silence ; on cessa de danser, et les violons ne jouèrent plus, tant on était attentif à contempler les grandes beautés de cet inconnue :
sentences.l: there made itself then a great silence; one ceased to dance, and the violins played no more, so much one was intent on contemplating the great beauties of this unknown [lady]:
sentences.i: A great silence fell; the dancing stopped and the violins played no more, so intent was everyone on gazing at the beauty of this unknown lady;
sentences.n: «il ſe fit un grand ſilence» ‘there made itself a great silence’ is impersonal: ‘a great silence fell’. «les violons» are the violinists, the string band that played for dancing, and «joüerent» (modern «jouèrent») is passé simple. «les grandes beautez» ‘the great beauties’ is her beauty in all its parts. The witness prints «cet inconnuë», a masculine «cet» with a feminine noun; the sense requires «cette inconnuë» ‘this unknown lady’, and Lectorium prints its witness unaltered. The literal line supplies ‘lady’ in brackets.

sentences.t: on n’entendoit qu’un bruit confus, ha, qu’elle eſt belle !
sentences.say: on n’entendait qu’un bruit confus, ha, qu’elle est belle !
sentences.l: one heard only a confused noise, ah, how she is beautiful!
sentences.i: Nothing could be heard but a confused murmur: Ah, how beautiful she is!
sentences.n: «ne … que» again: «on n’entendoit que» is ‘one heard only’. A «bruit confus» is a murmur of many voices at once. «qu’elle eſt belle !» is an exclamation in which «que» is ‘how’, and «ha» is ‘ah’, a spelling French still uses beside «ah».

sentences.t: Le Roi même tout vieux qu’il eſtoit, ne laiſſoit pas de la regarder, & de dire tout bas à la Reine, qu’il y avoit long-temps qu’il n’avoit vû une ſi belle & ſi aimable perſonne.
sentences.say: Le Roi même tout vieux qu’il était, ne laissait pas de la regarder, et de dire tout bas à la Reine, qu’il y avait longtemps qu’il n’avait vu une si belle et si aimable personne.
sentences.l: The King himself, all old that he was, did not leave off looking at her, and saying very low to the Queen, that it was a long time that he had not seen so beautiful and so lovable a person.
sentences.i: The King himself, old as he was, could not stop looking at her, and kept whispering to the Queen that it was a long time since he had seen so lovely and so charming a young woman.
sentences.n: «tout vieux qu’il eſtoit» ‘all old that he was’ is ‘old as he was’. «ne laiſſoit pas de» is ‘did not fail to, could not help’, the turn used of Cendrillon’s beauty in rags. «tout bas» is ‘very quietly’. «il y avoit long-temps qu’il n’avoit vû» ‘there was a long time that he had not seen’ is the French way of saying ‘it had been a long time since he had seen’. «aimable» is ‘lovable, charming’, warmer than English ‘amiable’, and «vû» is «vu», with a circumflex the modern word has dropped.

sentences.t: Toutes les Dames eſtoient attentives à conſiderer ſa coëffure & ſes habits, pour en avoir dés le lendemain de ſemblables, pourveu qu’il ſe trouvaſt des étoffes aſſez belles & des ouvriers aſſez habiles.
sentences.say: Toutes les Dames étaient attentives à considérer sa coiffure et ses habits, pour en avoir dès le lendemain de semblables, pourvu qu’il se trouvât des étoffes assez belles et des ouvriers assez habiles.
sentences.l: All the ladies were intent on considering her headdress and her clothes, so as to have some like them from the very next day, provided that there were found fabrics fine enough and workmen skilful enough.
sentences.i: All the ladies were intent on examining her headdress and her gown, so as to have the like made the very next day, provided that fine enough stuffs and skilful enough workmen could be found.
sentences.n: «conſiderer» in 1697 is ‘to look at closely, to scrutinise’, not only ‘to think about’. In «pour en avoir … de ſemblables» ‘to have like ones of them’, «en» is ‘of them’. «dés le lendemain» (modern «dès le lendemain») is ‘as early as the next day’. «pourveu que» (modern «pourvu que») ‘provided that’ takes the subjunctive, here the imperfect subjunctive «trouvaſt» (modern «trouvât»), and «il ſe trouvaſt» is ‘there should be found’. The «ouvriers» are the craftsmen, the tailors and dressmakers.

sentences.t: Le Fils du Roi la mit à la place la plus honorable, & enſuite la prit pour la mener danſer :
sentences.say: Le Fils du Roi la mit à la place la plus honorable, et ensuite la prit pour la mener danser :
sentences.l: The King’s son put her in the most honourable place, and then took her to lead her [to] dance:
sentences.i: The King’s son seated her in the place of highest honour, and then took her out to dance;
sentences.n: At a ball where one sat was fixed by rank, and «la place la plus honorable» was the seat of highest honour. «mener danſer» ‘to lead dance’ is ‘to lead out to dance’, «mener» with a bare infinitive; the literal line supplies ‘to’ in brackets. «mit» and «prit» are passé simple.

sentences.t: elle dança avec tant de grace, qu’on l’admira encore davantage.
sentences.say: elle dansa avec tant de grâce, qu’on l’admira encore davantage.
sentences.l: she danced with so much grace, that one admired her still more.
sentences.i: she danced so gracefully that she was admired more than ever.
sentences.n: «dança» (modern «dansa») is the passé simple of «danſer», printed with a ç. «tant de … que» is ‘so much … that’. «grace» lacks the circumflex of «grâce», and «davantage» is ‘more’.

sentences.t: On apporta une fort belle collation, dont le jeune Prince ne mangea point, tant il eſtoit occupé à la conſiderer.
sentences.say: On apporta une fort belle collation, dont le jeune Prince ne mangea point, tant il était occupé à la considérer.
sentences.l: One brought a very fine collation, of which the young Prince ate not at all, so much he was occupied in considering her.
sentences.i: A very fine collation was brought in, of which the young Prince ate nothing, so taken up was he with gazing at her.
sentences.n: A «collation» was a light meal of fruit, sweetmeats and cold dishes, served at a ball or late in the evening. «fort» before an adjective is ‘very’. In «dont … ne mangea point» ‘of which … ate not at all’, «dont» is ‘of which’ and «ne … point» a firm ‘not’. «occupé à la conſiderer» is ‘busy looking at her’.

sentences.t: Elle alla s’aſſeoir auprés de ſes ſœurs, & leur fit mille honneſtetez :
sentences.say: Elle alla s’asseoir auprès de ses sœurs, et leur fit mille honnêtetés :
sentences.l: She went to sit down near her sisters, and did them a thousand courtesies:
sentences.i: She went and sat beside her sisters and showed them every kind of courtesy;
sentences.n: «auprés de» (modern «auprès de») is ‘beside, near’. «honneſtetez» (modern «honnêtetés») were ‘courtesies, civilities’: in 1697 «honnêteté» was good manners, not honesty. «mille» ‘a thousand’ is simply ‘a great many’. The sisters do not know her.

sentences.t: elle leur fit part des oranges & des citrons que le Prince luy avoit donnez ; ce qui les eſtonna fort, car elles ne la connoiſſoient point.
sentences.say: elle leur fit part des oranges et des citrons que le Prince lui avait donnez ; ce qui les étonna fort, car elles ne la connaissaient point.
sentences.l: she gave them share of the oranges and the lemons that the Prince had given her; which astonished them greatly, for they did not know her at all.
sentences.i: she shared with them the oranges and lemons the Prince had given her, which amazed them, for they had no idea who she was.
sentences.n: «faire part de» is ‘to give a share of’. Oranges and lemons, brought up from the south, were costly delicacies in the France of 1697, and to be given them by the Prince was a mark of favour. «eſtonna» (modern «étonna») is ‘astonished’, and «donnez» is «donnés», agreeing with the fruit.

sentences.t: Lorſqu’elles cauſoient ainſi, Cendrillon entendit ſonner onze heures trois quarts ;
sentences.say: Lorsqu’elles causaient ainsi, Cendrillon entendit sonner onze heures trois quarts ;
sentences.l: While they were chatting thus, Cendrillon heard strike eleven hours three quarters;
sentences.i: While they were talking in this way, Cinderella heard the clock strike a quarter to twelve;
sentences.n: «cauſer» is ‘to chat’. «entendre ſonner» ‘to hear strike’ is ‘to hear (the clock) strike’, with an infinitive after a verb of hearing. «onze heures trois quarts» ‘eleven hours three quarters’ is how French tells the time at a quarter to midnight.

sentences.t: elle fit auſſi-toſt une grande reverence à la compagnie, & s’en alla le plus viſte qu’elle pût.
sentences.say: elle fit aussitôt une grande révérence à la compagnie, et s’en alla le plus vite qu’elle pût.
sentences.l: she made at once a great curtsey to the company, and went away the fastest that she could.
sentences.i: at once she made a deep curtsey to the company and left as fast as she could.
sentences.n: A «reverence» (modern «révérence») is a curtsey or a bow, and «une grande reverence» a deep one, as manners required on taking leave. «s’en aller» is ‘to go away’, and «viſte» is «vite» ‘fast’. «pût» is the imperfect subjunctive of «pouvoir», which literary French may use after «le plus … que»; a little earlier the tale has the plain «put» in the same turn.

sentences.t: Dés qu’elle fut arrivée, elle alla trouver ſa Maraine, & aprés l’avoir remerciée, elle luy dit qu’elle ſouhaiteroit bien aller encore le lendemain au Bal, parce que le Fils du Roi l’en avoit priée.
sentences.say: Dès qu’elle fut arrivée, elle alla trouver sa Marraine, et après l’avoir remerciée, elle lui dit qu’elle souhaiterait bien aller encore le lendemain au Bal, parce que le Fils du Roi l’en avait priée.
sentences.l: As soon as she was arrived, she went to find her godmother, and after having thanked her, she said to her that she would well wish to go again the next day to the ball, because the King’s son had asked her [to].
sentences.i: As soon as she was home she went to find her godmother, and when she had thanked her she told her that she would dearly like to go to the ball again the next day, because the King’s son had asked her to.
sentences.n: «Dés qu’elle fut arrivée» ‘as soon as she was arrived’ is the past anterior of «arriver», which takes «être», and «dés» is «dès». «aller trouver» ‘to go find’ is ‘to go to (someone)’. «ſouhaiteroit bien» (modern «souhaiterait») is ‘would very much wish’. In «l’en avoit priée» ‘had asked her of it’, «prier» is again ‘to ask, to invite’ and «en» stands for going to the ball; the literal line supplies ‘to’ in brackets.

sentences.t: Comme elle eſtoit occupée à raconter à ſa Maraine tout ce qui s’étoit paſſé au bal, les deux ſœurs heurterent à la porte ;
sentences.say: Comme elle était occupée à raconter à sa Marraine tout ce qui s’était passé au bal, les deux sœurs heurtèrent à la porte ;
sentences.l: As she was occupied in recounting to her godmother all that had passed at the ball, the two sisters knocked at the door;
sentences.i: While she was busy telling her godmother everything that had happened at the ball, the two sisters knocked at the door;
sentences.n: «ſe paſſer» is ‘to happen, to take place’. «heurter à la porte» is ‘to knock at the door’, an older sense of «heurter» ‘to strike’. The witness prints «s’étoit» with the modern «é» but the old «-oit» ending, beside its usual «eſtoit».

sentences.t: Cendrillon leur alla ouvrir : Que vous eſtes longtemps à revenir, leur dit-elle, en bâillant, en ſe frottant les yeux, & en s’étendant comme ſi elle n’euſt fait que de ſe réveiller :
sentences.say: Cendrillon leur alla ouvrir : Que vous êtes longtemps à revenir, leur dit-elle, en bâillant, en se frottant les yeux, et en s’étendant comme si elle n’eût fait que de se réveiller :
sentences.l: Cendrillon went to open to them: How you are long in coming back, she said to them, yawning, rubbing her eyes, and stretching as if she had done nothing but wake up:
sentences.i: Cinderella went to let them in. How long you have been in coming back! she said, yawning, rubbing her eyes and stretching as though she had only just woken up;
sentences.n: «leur alla ouvrir» ‘went to open to them’ keeps the pronoun before «alla», the 1697 order. «Que vous eſtes longtemps à revenir» ‘how you are long in coming back’ is an exclamation with «que» ‘how’, and Cendrillon says «vous» to her stepsisters, as before. «ne faire que de» with an infinitive is ‘to have only just (done)’, and «n’euſt fait» (modern «n’eût fait») is the pluperfect subjunctive after «comme ſi», built on the imperfect subjunctive of «avoir». She is play-acting, as the next clause makes plain.

sentences.t: elle n’avoit cependant pas eu envie de dormir depuis qu’elles s’eſtoient quittées :
sentences.say: elle n’avait cependant pas eu envie de dormir depuis qu’elles s’étaient quittées :
sentences.l: she had however not had desire to sleep since they had left each other:
sentences.i: and yet she had felt no wish to sleep since they had parted;
sentences.n: «avoir envie de» is ‘to feel like, to want to’. «cependant» ‘however’ is the narrator’s dry aside. «s’eſtoient quittées» ‘had left each other’ is reciprocal: she and the sisters had last parted at the ball.

sentences.t: Si tu eſtois venuë au Bal, luy dit une de ſes ſœurs, tu ne t’y ſerais pas ennuyée ;
sentences.say: Si tu étais venue au Bal, lui dit une de ses sœurs, tu ne t’y serais pas ennuyée ;
sentences.l: If you had come to the ball, one of her sisters said to her, you would not have been bored there;
sentences.i: If you had come to the ball, one of her sisters told her, you would not have found it dull;
sentences.n: «Si tu eſtois venuë … tu ne t’y ſerais pas ennuyée» ‘if you had come … you would not have been bored there’ sets a pluperfect after «ſi» and a conditional perfect in the main clause; «venir» and «s’ennuyer» both take «être», and the participles agree with Cendrillon. «ſerais» is printed with the modern ending, beside «eſtois» with the old one. The sister says «tu».

sentences.t: il y eſt venu la plus belle Princeſſe, la plus belle qu’on puiſſe jamais voir ; elle nous a fait mille civilitez ; elle nous a donné des oranges & des citrons.
sentences.say: il y est venu la plus belle Princesse, la plus belle qu’on puisse jamais voir ; elle nous a fait mille civilités ; elle nous a donné des oranges et des citrons.
sentences.l: there has come there the most beautiful princess, the most beautiful that one could ever see; she has done us a thousand civilities; she has given us some oranges and some lemons.
sentences.i: The loveliest princess came, the loveliest anyone could ever see; she was all courtesy to us, and she gave us oranges and lemons.
sentences.n: The sisters speak in the passé composé, «eſt venu», «a fait», «a donné», the past of conversation, where the narrator uses the passé simple. «il y eſt venu la plus belle Princeſſe» ‘there has come there the most beautiful princess’ is impersonal, with the verb left masculine singular. «qu’on puiſſe jamais voir» has the subjunctive after a superlative, and «civilitez» (modern «civilités») are courtesies. They boast of the very fruit Cendrillon gave them.

sentences.t: Cendrillon ne ſe ſentoit pas de joye : elle leur demanda le nom de cette Princeſſe ;
sentences.say: Cendrillon ne se sentait pas de joie : elle leur demanda le nom de cette Princesse ;
sentences.l: Cendrillon did not feel herself for joy: she asked them the name of this princess;
sentences.i: Cinderella was beside herself with joy; she asked them the princess’s name;
sentences.n: «ne ſe ſentoit pas de joye» is ‘was beside herself with joy’, the phrase used as she set off for the ball; the imperfect makes it her state as she listens. «demanda» is passé simple.

sentences.t: mais elles luy répondirent qu’on ne la connoiſſoit pas, que le Fils du Roi en eſtoit fort en peine, & qu’il donneroit toutes choſes au monde pour ſçavoir qui elle eſtoit.
sentences.say: mais elles lui répondirent qu’on ne la connaissait pas, que le Fils du Roi en était fort en peine, et qu’il donnerait toutes choses au monde pour savoir qui elle était.
sentences.l: but they answered her that one did not know her, that the King’s son was very troubled about it, and that he would give all things in the world to know who she was.
sentences.i: but they told her that nobody knew her, that the King’s son was sorely troubled about it, and that he would give anything in the world to find out who she was.
sentences.n: Their answer is reported in a string of «que» clauses. «eſtre en peine de» is ‘to be troubled about’, with «en» ‘about it’. «ſçavoir» is the 1697 spelling of «savoir» ‘to know’, its c added in the belief that the word came from Latin «scire». «donneroit» is «donnerait» ‘would give’.

sentences.t: Cendrillon ſourit & leur dit, elle eſtoit donc bien belle ?
sentences.say: Cendrillon sourit et leur dit, elle était donc bien belle ?
sentences.l: Cendrillon smiled and said to them, she was then very beautiful?
sentences.i: Cinderella smiled and said to them, So she was very beautiful?
sentences.n: «ſourit» ‘smiled’ is passé simple, though the present of «ſourire» has the same form. «donc» is ‘then, so’, and «bien belle» is ‘very beautiful’. The question is a plain statement with a question mark, as spoken French often makes it.

sentences.t: Mon Dieu ! que vous eſtes heureuſes, ne pourrois-je point la voir ?
sentences.say: Mon Dieu ! que vous êtes heureuses, ne pourrais-je point la voir ?
sentences.l: My God! how you are fortunate, could I not see her?
sentences.i: Heavens, how lucky you are! Might I not see her?
sentences.n: «Mon Dieu !» is an everyday exclamation, ‘Heavens!’. «heureuſes» is ‘fortunate, lucky’ as much as ‘happy’. «ne pourrois-je point» (modern «ne pourrais-je pas») ‘could I not’ is a wistful question, and she is playing a game with them, as the next lines show.

sentences.t: Helas ! Mademoiſelle Javote, preſtez-moi voſtre habit jaune que vous mettez tous les jours :
sentences.say: Hélas ! Mademoiselle Javote, prêtez-moi votre habit jaune que vous mettez tous les jours :
sentences.l: Alas! Mademoiselle Javote, lend me your yellow gown that you wear every day:
sentences.i: Oh, Mademoiselle Javote, do lend me that yellow gown you wear every day!
sentences.n: «Javote», printed «Javotte» a line later, is one of the sisters, named here for the first time; the name, a homely one of the period, stays French. «Mademoiſelle» is the title Cendrillon owes her. «preſtez» (modern «prêtez») is a «vous» imperative, ‘lend’, and «voſtre» is «votre». The gown she asks for is the one Javotte wears every day, not her ball finery. «Helas» lacks the accent of «hélas».

sentences.t: vraiment, dit mademoiſelle Javotte, je ſuis de cet avis, preſtez voſtre habit à un vilain Cucendron comme cela, il faudroit que je fuſſe bien folle.
sentences.say: vraiment, dit mademoiselle Javotte, je suis de cet avis, prêtez votre habit à un vilain Cucendron comme cela, il faudrait que je fusse bien folle.
sentences.l: truly, said Mademoiselle Javotte, I am of that opinion, lend your gown to a nasty Cucendron like that, it would be needful that I were very mad.
sentences.i: Indeed! said Mademoiselle Javotte. What a fine idea: lend your gown to a filthy Cucendron like that! I should have to be quite mad.
sentences.n: «vraiment» ‘truly’ is scornful here, and «je ſuis de cet avis» ‘I am of that opinion’ is sarcasm, meaning the opposite. «preſtez voſtre habit» throws Cendrillon’s own words back at her, which is why it keeps «vous» and «voſtre». «il faudroit que je fuſſe bien folle» ‘it would be needful that I were very mad’: after «il faudroit que» (modern «il faudrait que») the verb goes into the imperfect subjunctive, «fuſſe». «vilain» is ‘nasty, dirty’, and still carried a sense of ‘base, low-born’. The witness spells the name «Javotte» here and prints «mademoiſelle» in lower case.

sentences.t: Cendrillon s’attendoit bien à ce refus, & elle en fut bien aiſe, car elle auroit eſté grandement embarraſſée ſi ſa ſœur eut bien voulu luy preſter ſon habit.
sentences.say: Cendrillon s’attendait bien à ce refus, et elle en fut bien aise, car elle aurait été grandement embarrassée si sa sœur eut bien voulu lui prêter son habit.
sentences.l: Cendrillon fully expected this refusal, and she was well glad of it, for she would have been greatly embarrassed if her sister had been willing to lend her her gown.
sentences.i: Cinderella had fully expected this refusal, and she was glad of it, for she would have been in great difficulty if her sister had been willing to lend her the gown.
sentences.n: «s’attendre à» is ‘to expect’, with «bien» ‘fully’. «embarraſſée» is ‘in a fix, awkwardly placed’, more than English ‘embarrassed’. «ſi ſa ſœur eut bien voulu» stands for «eût bien voulu» ‘had been willing’, the pluperfect subjunctive that literary French could use after «ſi» where modern French says «avait voulu»; «vouloir bien» is ‘to be willing’ again. «auroit eſté» is «aurait été» ‘would have been’.

sentences.t: Le lendemain, les deux ſœurs furent au bal, & Cendrillon auſſi, mais encore plus parée que la premiere fois.
sentences.say: Le lendemain, les deux sœurs furent au bal, et Cendrillon aussi, mais encore plus parée que la première fois.
sentences.l: The next day, the two sisters were at the ball, and Cendrillon also, but even more adorned than the first time.
sentences.i: The next day the two sisters went to the ball, and so did Cinderella, dressed even more splendidly than the first time.
sentences.n: «furent au bal» ‘were at the ball’: the passé simple of «être» with «à» can mean ‘went to’, and the idiomatic line takes it so. «parée» is ‘adorned’ again, and «premiere» lacks its grave accent.

sentences.t: Le Fils du Roi fut toûjours auprés d’elle, & ne ceſſa de lui conter des douceurs ;
sentences.say: Le Fils du Roi fut toujours auprès d’elle, et ne cessa de lui conter des douceurs ;
sentences.l: The King’s son was always near her, and ceased not to tell her sweet things;
sentences.i: The King’s son never left her side, and did not stop paying her tender compliments;
sentences.n: «fut toûjours auprés d’elle» ‘was always near her’ is ‘stayed by her side the whole time’. «ne ceſſa de» ‘ceased not to’: with «ceſſer», as with «oſer», French may leave out the «pas». «conter des douceurs» ‘to tell sweetnesses’ is to pay a woman tender compliments. «lui» is again in its modern spelling.

sentences.t: la jeune Demoiſelle ne s’ennuyoit point & oublia ce que ſa Maraine luy avoit recommandé ;
sentences.say: la jeune Demoiselle ne s’ennuyait point et oublia ce que sa Marraine lui avait recommandé ;
sentences.l: the young lady was not bored at all and forgot what her godmother had enjoined her;
sentences.i: the young lady was far from bored, and she forgot what her godmother had charged her to do;
sentences.n: «ne s’ennuyoit point» ‘was not bored at all’ is understatement: she was enjoying herself. The imperfect «s’ennuyoit» is her state, and the passé simple «oublia» ‘forgot’ the event that comes of it. «recommandé» is the godmother’s charge not to stay past midnight.

sentences.t: de ſorte qu’elle entendit ſonner le premier coup de minuit, lorſqu’elle ne croyoit pas qui fut encore onze heures :
sentences.say: de sorte qu’elle entendit sonner le premier coup de minuit, lorsqu’elle ne croyait pas qui fut encore onze heures :
sentences.l: so that she heard strike the first stroke of midnight, when she did not believe that it was yet eleven hours:
sentences.i: so that she heard the first stroke of midnight when she thought it was not yet eleven;
sentences.n: «de ſorte que» is ‘so that’, and «le premier coup de minuit» ‘the first stroke of midnight’. The witness prints «qui fut», where the sense requires «qu’il fût» ‘that it was’, with «fût» in the imperfect subjunctive after «ne croyoit pas que»; in speech «qu’il» often sounded like «qui», which may explain the spelling, but whether it is the printer’s or the transcription’s, Lectorium prints its witness unaltered. «croyoit» is «croyait» ‘believed’.

sentences.t: elle ſe leva & s’enfüit auſſi legerement qu’auroit fait une biche :
sentences.say: elle se leva et s’enfuit aussi légèrement qu’aurait fait une biche :
sentences.l: she rose and fled as lightly as a doe would have done:
sentences.i: she rose and fled, as lightly as a deer might have done;
sentences.n: «ſe leva» ‘rose’ and «s’enfüit» ‘fled’ are passés simples; «s’enfuir» is ‘to run away’, and the diaeresis on its «ü» is the printer’s. «auſſi … qu’auroit fait une biche» ‘as … as a doe would have done’ puts the subject after the verb in the comparison. «legerement» is «légèrement» ‘lightly’.

sentences.t: le Prince la ſuivit, mais il ne put l’attraper ;
sentences.say: le Prince la suivit, mais il ne put l’attraper ;
sentences.l: the Prince followed her, but he could not catch her;
sentences.n: «ſuivit» is the passé simple of «ſuivre» ‘to follow’, and «put» that of «pouvoir»: «ne put» ‘could not’ leaves out «pas», as «pouvoir» may.

sentences.t: elle laiſſa tomber une de ſes pantoufles de verre, que le Prince ramaſſa bienſoigneuſement.
sentences.say: elle laissa tomber une de ses pantoufles de verre, que le Prince ramassa bien-soigneusement.
sentences.l: she let fall one of her slippers of glass, which the Prince picked up very carefully.
sentences.i: she let fall one of her glass slippers, which the Prince picked up with great care.
sentences.n: Each time the book says what the slippers are made of (three times in the tale, and once in the title) it prints «verre» ‘glass’, and Lectorium translates glass. The reading «vair», a squirrel fur whose name sounds the same, is a later conjecture with no support in this edition. The book spells the word both «pantoufle» and «pentoufle» (the first mention is «pentoufles de verre», and the title has «PENTOUFLE»); they are one word, modern «pantoufle», and «la petite pentoufle» is ‘the little slipper’. «laiſſer tomber» is ‘to let fall, to drop’, and «ramaſſer» ‘to pick up’. The witness runs «bien ſoigneuſement» ‘very carefully’ together as one word; whether the lost space is the printer’s or the transcription’s, Lectorium prints its witness unaltered.

sentences.t: Cendrillon arriva chez elle, bien éſoufflée, ſans caroſſe, ſans laquais, & avec ſes méchans habits, rien ne luy eſtant reſté de toute ſa magnificence, qu’une de ſes petites pantoufles, la pareille de celle qu’elle avoit laiſſé tomber.
sentences.say: Cendrillon arriva chez elle, bien essoufflée, sans carrosse, sans laquais, et avec ses méchants habits, rien ne lui étant resté de toute sa magnificence, qu’une de ses petites pantoufles, la pareille de celle qu’elle avait laissé tomber.
sentences.l: Cendrillon arrived at her home, well out of breath, without coach, without lackeys, and with her wretched clothes, nothing having remained to her of all her magnificence but one of her little slippers, the match of the one that she had let fall.
sentences.i: Cinderella reached home quite out of breath, with no coach and no footmen, in her shabby old clothes; nothing was left of all her splendour but one of her little slippers, the fellow of the one she had dropped.
sentences.n: «chez elle» is ‘at her home’. «éſoufflée» is «essoufflée» ‘out of breath’, printed with one s. «rien ne luy eſtant reſté … qu’une» ‘nothing remaining to her … but one’ pairs «rien» with «que» for ‘nothing but’. «la pareille» is ‘the match, the fellow’ of a pair. «laiſſé» does not agree before the infinitive «tomber». «méchans habits» are her ‘poor clothes’ once more.

sentences.t: On demanda aux Gardes de la porte du Palais s’ils n’avoient point veu ſortir une Princeſſe ;
sentences.say: On demanda aux Gardes de la porte du Palais s’ils n’avaient point vu sortir une Princesse ;
sentences.l: One asked the guards of the gate of the palace if they had not seen a princess go out;
