sentences.i: The guards at the palace gate were asked whether they had seen a princess go out;
sentences.n: «On demanda aux Gardes» ‘one asked the guards’ leaves unsaid who asked, and the English passive does the same. «veu ſortir» (modern «vu sortir») ‘seen go out’ is a verb of seeing with an infinitive. «s’ils n’avoient point veu» ‘if they had not seen’ is a way of asking whether.

sentences.t: ils dirent qu’ils n’avoient veu ſortir perſonne, qu’une jeune fille fort mal veſtuë, & qui avoit plus l’air d’une Payſanne que d’une Demoiſelle.
sentences.say: ils dirent qu’ils n’avaient vu sortir personne, qu’une jeune fille fort mal vêtue, et qui avait plus l’air d’une Paysanne que d’une Demoiselle.
sentences.l: they said that they had seen nobody go out, but a young girl very badly dressed, and who had more the air of a peasant girl than of a young lady.
sentences.i: they said they had seen no one go out but a very poorly dressed girl, who looked more like a peasant than a young lady.
sentences.n: «ne … perſonne» is ‘nobody’, and «qu’une jeune fille» ‘but a young girl’ adds «que» ‘except’. «mal veſtuë» (modern «mal vêtue») is ‘badly dressed’, and «avoir l’air de» is ‘to look like’. A «Payſanne» (modern «paysanne») was a country girl of the labouring sort, a «Demoiſelle» a girl of good family: the guards judge by dress alone.

sentences.t: Quand les deux ſœurs revinrent du Bal, Cendrillon leur demanda ſi elles s’eſtoient encore bien diverties, & ſi la belle Dame y avoit eſté ;
sentences.say: Quand les deux sœurs revinrent du Bal, Cendrillon leur demanda si elles s’étaient encore bien diverties, et si la belle Dame y avait été ;
sentences.l: When the two sisters came back from the ball, Cendrillon asked them if they had again enjoyed themselves well, and if the beautiful lady had been there;
sentences.i: When the two sisters came home from the ball, Cinderella asked them whether they had enjoyed themselves again, and whether the beautiful lady had been there;
sentences.n: «revinrent» is the passé simple of «revenir» ‘to come back’. «ſe divertir» is ‘to enjoy oneself’, and «s’eſtoient … diverties» agrees with the sisters. In «y avoit eſté» ‘had been there’, «y» is the ball. Cendrillon asks with a straight face.

sentences.t: elles luy dirent que oüy, mais qu’elle s’étoit enfuye lorſque minuit avoit ſonné, & ſi promptement qu’elle avoit laiſſé tomber une de ſes petites pantoufles de verre, la plus jolie du monde ;
sentences.say: elles lui dirent que oui, mais qu’elle s’était enfuie lorsque minuit avait sonné, et si promptement qu’elle avait laissé tomber une de ses petites pantoufles de verre, la plus jolie du monde ;
sentences.l: they told her that yes, but that she had fled when midnight had struck, and so promptly that she had let fall one of her little slippers of glass, the prettiest in the world;
sentences.i: they told her yes, but that she had run away as midnight struck, and so hastily that she had dropped one of her little glass slippers, the prettiest in the world;
sentences.n: Each time the book says what the slippers are made of (three times in the tale, and once in the title) it prints «verre» ‘glass’, and Lectorium translates glass. The reading «vair», a squirrel fur whose name sounds the same, is a later conjecture with no support in this edition. The book spells the word both «pantoufle» and «pentoufle» (the first mention is «pentoufles de verre», and the title has «PENTOUFLE»); they are one word, modern «pantoufle», and «la petite pentoufle» is ‘the little slipper’. «dire que oüy» ‘to say that yes’ is ‘to say yes’, and «oüy» is «oui». «s’étoit enfuye» (modern «s’était enfuie») is ‘had fled’.

sentences.t: que le fils du Roy l’avoit ramaſſée, & qu’il n’avoit fait que la regarder pendant tout le reſte du Bal, & qu’aſſurément il eſtoit fort amoureux de la belle perſonne à qui appartenoit la petite pentoufle.
sentences.say: que le fils du Roi l’avait ramassée, et qu’il n’avait fait que la regarder pendant tout le reste du Bal, et qu’assurément il était fort amoureux de la belle personne à qui appartenait la petite pantoufle.
sentences.l: that the King’s son had picked it up, and that he had done nothing but look at it during all the rest of the ball, and that assuredly he was very much in love with the beautiful person to whom belonged the little slipper.
sentences.i: that the King’s son had picked it up and had done nothing but gaze at it for the rest of the ball, and that he was certainly deeply in love with the beautiful lady to whom the little slipper belonged.
sentences.n: The report goes on in «que» clauses. In «n’avoit fait que la regarder» ‘had done nothing but look at it’, «la» is the slipper. «à qui appartenoit la petite pentoufle» ‘to whom belonged the little slipper’ puts the subject after the verb. «Roy», with the 1697 y, and «pentoufle», the book’s other spelling of «pantoufle», are both printed here.

sentences.t: Elles dirent vray, car peu de jours aprés, le fils du Roy fit publier à ſon de trompe, qu’il épouſeroit celle dont le pied ſeroit bien juſte à la pentoufle.
sentences.say: Elles dirent vrai, car peu de jours après, le fils du Roi fit publier à son de trompe, qu’il épouserait celle dont le pied serait bien juste à la pantoufle.
sentences.l: They said true, for few days after, the King’s son caused to be proclaimed by sound of trumpet, that he would marry her whose foot would be quite exact to the slipper.
sentences.i: They spoke the truth, for a few days later the King’s son had it proclaimed by sound of trumpet that he would marry the woman whose foot the slipper fitted exactly.
sentences.n: «dire vray» (modern «dire vrai») is ‘to speak the truth’. «fit publier» ‘caused to be proclaimed, had (it) proclaimed’ is «faire» with an infinitive, and «à ſon de trompe» ‘by sound of trumpet’ is how public announcements were made, a trumpet calling people to hear them. «celle dont le pied» ‘her whose foot’ uses «dont» for ‘whose’. «juſte» is ‘exactly fitting’, a sense the word still has in French of clothes and shoes.

sentences.t: On commença à l’eſſayer aux Princeſſes, enſuite aux Ducheſſes, & à toute la Cour, mais inutilement :
sentences.say: On commença à l’essayer aux Princesses, ensuite aux Duchesses, et à toute la Cour, mais inutilement :
sentences.l: One began to try it on the princesses, then on the duchesses, and on all the Court, but uselessly:
sentences.i: They began by trying it on the princesses, then on the duchesses and the whole Court, but in vain;
sentences.n: «eſſayer quelque choſe à quelqu’un» is ‘to try something on someone’. The order is the order of rank: princesses first, then duchesses, then the rest of the Court. «inutilement» is ‘in vain’.

sentences.t: on la porta chez les deux ſœurs, qui firent tout leur poſſible pour faire entrer leur pied dans la pentoufle, mais elles ne purent en venir à bout.
sentences.say: on la porta chez les deux sœurs, qui firent tout leur possible pour faire entrer leur pied dans la pantoufle, mais elles ne purent en venir à bout.
sentences.l: one carried it to the house of the two sisters, who did all their possible to make their foot go into the slipper, but they could not come to the end of it.
sentences.i: it was brought to the two sisters, who did all they could to get their feet into the slipper, but they could not manage it.
sentences.n: «chez» is ‘at the house of’. «faire tout leur poſſible» is ‘to do their utmost’, and «faire entrer leur pied» ‘to make their foot go in’ is «faire» with an infinitive. «en venir à bout» ‘to come to the end of it’ is ‘to succeed, to manage’; the verse moral takes the phrase up again.

sentences.t: Cendrillon, qui les regardoit, & qui reconnut ſa pentoufle, dit en riant, que je voye ſi elle ne me ſerait pas bonne :
sentences.say: Cendrillon, qui les regardait, et qui reconnut sa pantoufle, dit en riant, que je voie si elle ne me serait pas bonne :
sentences.l: Cendrillon, who was watching them, and who recognised her slipper, said laughing, let me see if it would not be good on me:
sentences.i: Cinderella, who was watching them and knew her slipper, said with a laugh, Let me see whether it might not fit me.
sentences.n: The imperfect «regardoit» ‘was watching’ is the background, and the passés simples «reconnut», «dit» are what happens against it. «que je voye» ‘that I may see’ is a subjunctive standing alone as a request, ‘let me see’, and «voye» is «voie». «ſi elle ne me ſerait pas bonne» ‘if it would not be good for me’ is ‘whether it might not fit me’; «ſerait» is printed with the modern ending.

sentences.t: ſes ſœurs ſe mirent à rire et à ſe moquer d’elle.
sentences.say: ses sœurs se mirent à rire et à se moquer d’elle.
sentences.l: her sisters set themselves to laughing and to mocking her.
sentences.i: her sisters began to laugh and make fun of her.
sentences.n: «ſe mettre à» ‘to set oneself to’ is ‘to begin to’, as when Cendrillon began to weep. «ſe moquer de» is ‘to make fun of’, spelt here with one c, where the tale earlier printed «mocquez».

sentences.t: Le Gentilhomme qui faiſoit l’aſſay de la pentoufle, ayant regardé attentivement Cendrillon, & la trouvant fort belle, dit que cela eſtoit juſte, & qu’il avoit ordre de l’eſſayer à toutes les filles :
sentences.say: Le Gentilhomme qui faisait l’essai de la pantoufle, ayant regardé attentivement Cendrillon, et la trouvant fort belle, dit que cela était juste, et qu’il avait ordre de l’essayer à toutes les filles :
sentences.l: The gentleman who was making the trial of the slipper, having looked attentively at Cendrillon, and finding her very beautiful, said that that was just, and that he had order to try it on all the girls:
sentences.i: The gentleman who was conducting the trial of the slipper looked closely at Cinderella and, finding her very beautiful, said that this was only fair, and that he had orders to try it on every girl;
sentences.n: «faire l’aſſay de» is ‘to make the trial of’, «aſſay» being an old spelling of «essai» ‘trial’. «juſte» here is ‘fair, right’, and the tale has just used the same word of a slipper that fits. «avoir ordre de» is ‘to have orders to’. A «Gentilhomme» is a man of noble birth, here one of the Prince’s household.

sentences.t: il fit aſſeoir Cendrillon, & approchant la pentoufle de ſon petit pied, il vit qu’elle y entroit ſanspeine, et qu’elle y eſtoit juſte comme de cire.
sentences.say: il fit asseoir Cendrillon, et approchant la pantoufle de son petit pied, il vit qu’elle y entrait sans-peine, et qu’elle y était juste comme de cire.
sentences.l: he made Cendrillon sit, and bringing the slipper near her little foot, he saw that it went on without trouble, and that it was as exact on it as [if] of wax.
sentences.i: he had Cinderella sit down, and as he brought the slipper to her little foot he saw that it slipped on without the least trouble and fitted as if it had been moulded in wax.
sentences.n: «fit aſſeoir» ‘made sit’ is «faire» with an infinitive, ‘had her sit down’. «approcher quelque choſe de» is ‘to bring something near to’. The witness runs «ſans peine» ‘without difficulty’ together as one word; whether the lost space is the printer’s or the transcription’s, Lectorium prints its witness unaltered. «juſte comme de cire» ‘exact as of wax’ is a set phrase for a perfect fit, as if moulded in wax; the literal line supplies ‘if’ in brackets. «entroit» is «entrait».

sentences.t: L’étonnement des deux ſœurs fut grand, mais plus grand encore quand Cendrillon tira de ſa poche l’autre petite pentoufle, qu’elle mit à ſon pied.
sentences.say: L’étonnement des deux sœurs fut grand, mais plus grand encore quand Cendrillon tira de sa poche l’autre petite pantoufle, qu’elle mit à son pied.
sentences.l: The astonishment of the two sisters was great, but greater still when Cendrillon drew from her pocket the other little slipper, which she put on her foot.
sentences.i: Great was the two sisters’ astonishment, and greater still when Cinderella took the other little slipper out of her pocket and put it on.
sentences.n: «tirer de» is ‘to draw out of, to take out of’. «qu’elle mit à ſon pied» ‘which she put to her foot’ is ‘which she put on’, with «mit» the passé simple of «mettre». «fut» ‘was’ serves both halves: the astonishment was great, then greater.

sentences.t: Là-deſſus arriva la Maraine, qui, ayant donné un coup de ſa baguette ſur les habits de Cendrillon, les fit devenir encore plus magnifiques que tous les autres.
sentences.say: Là-dessus arriva la Marraine, qui, ayant donné un coup de sa baguette sur les habits de Cendrillon, les fit devenir encore plus magnifiques que tous les autres.
sentences.l: Thereupon arrived the godmother, who, having given a stroke of her wand on the clothes of Cendrillon, made them become still more magnificent than all the others.
sentences.i: At that moment the godmother arrived, and with a touch of her wand upon Cinderella’s clothes she made them more magnificent even than all the others.
sentences.n: «Là-deſſus» (modern «là-dessus») is ‘thereupon, at that’, and «arriva la Maraine» puts the subject after its verb, as French may after an opening adverb. «les fit devenir» ‘made them become’ is «faire» with an infinitive once more. «tous les autres» ‘all the others’ are the gowns she wore to the two balls.

sentences.t: Alors ſes deux ſœurs la reconnurent pour la belle perſonne qu’elles avoient veuë au Bal.
sentences.say: Alors ses deux sœurs la reconnurent pour la belle personne qu’elles avaient vue au Bal.
sentences.l: Then her two sisters recognised her for the beautiful person whom they had seen at the ball.
sentences.i: Then her two sisters knew her for the beautiful lady they had seen at the ball.
sentences.n: «reconnoître pour» (here «reconnurent», passé simple) is ‘to recognise as’. «veuë» agrees with «qu’», standing for «la belle perſonne», the object set before it: ‘whom they had seen’.

sentences.t: Elles ſe jetterent à ſes pieds pour luy demander pardon de tous les mauvais traittemens, qu’elles luy avoient fait ſouffrir.
sentences.say: Elles se jetèrent à ses pieds pour lui demander pardon de tous les mauvais traitements, qu’elles lui avaient fait souffrir.
sentences.l: They threw themselves at her feet to ask her pardon for all the ill treatments that they had made her suffer.
sentences.i: They threw themselves at her feet to beg her forgiveness for all the ill-treatment they had made her suffer.
sentences.n: «jetterent» (modern «jetèrent») and «traittemens» (modern «traitements») are 1697 spellings with a doubled consonant, and «traittemens» also drops the t of its plural. «demander pardon de» is ‘to ask forgiveness for’. «fait ſouffrir» ‘made suffer’ is «faire» with an infinitive, and «ſouffrir» here is ‘to suffer, to endure’.

sentences.t: Cendrillon les releva et leur dit, en les embraſſant, qu’elle leur pardonnoit de bon cœur, & qu’elle les prioit de l’aimer bien toûjours.
sentences.say: Cendrillon les releva et leur dit, en les embrassant, qu’elle leur pardonnait de bon cœur, et qu’elle les priait de l’aimer bien toujours.
sentences.l: Cendrillon raised them up and said to them, embracing them, that she forgave them with good heart, and that she begged them to love her well always.
sentences.i: Cinderella raised them up and, embracing them, told them that she forgave them with all her heart, and begged them always to love her dearly.
sentences.n: «relever» is ‘to raise up’ someone who has knelt. «embraſſer» is ‘to take in one’s arms’, from «bras» ‘arm’, not ‘to kiss’. «pardonner à quelqu’un» takes «à», hence «leur» ‘to them’. «de bon cœur» is ‘with all her heart’, and «prier» here is ‘to beg’.

sentences.t: On la mena chez le jeune Prince, parée comme elle eſtoit :
sentences.say: On la mena chez le jeune Prince, parée comme elle était :
sentences.l: One led her to the young Prince, adorned as she was:
sentences.i: She was taken to the young Prince, arrayed just as she was;
sentences.n: «On la mena» ‘one led her’ leaves the escort unnamed, and the English passive does the same. «chez» is ‘to the house of’, here the Prince’s palace. «parée comme elle eſtoit» is ‘in all her finery, just as she was’.

sentences.t: il la trouva encore plus belle que jamais, & peu de jours aprés il l’épouſa.
sentences.say: il la trouva encore plus belle que jamais, et peu de jours après il l’épousa.
sentences.l: he found her still more beautiful than ever, and few days after he married her.
sentences.i: he found her more beautiful than ever, and a few days later he married her.
sentences.n: «trouver» with an adjective is ‘to find (someone) so’, to think her so. «peu de jours aprés» ‘few days after’ is ‘a few days later’, and «aprés» is «après». «épouſa» is the passé simple of «épouſer» ‘to marry’, the verb the tale opened with.

sentences.t: Cendrillon, qui eſtoit auſſi bonne que belle, fit loger ſes deux ſœurs au Palais, et les maria dés le jour même à deux grands Seigneurs de la Cour.
sentences.say: Cendrillon, qui était aussi bonne que belle, fit loger ses deux sœurs au Palais, et les maria dès le jour même à deux grands Seigneurs de la Cour.
sentences.l: Cendrillon, who was as good as beautiful, had her two sisters lodged at the palace, and married them that very day to two great lords of the Court.
sentences.i: Cinderella, who was as good as she was beautiful, gave her two sisters lodgings in the palace, and that very same day married them to two great lords of the Court.
sentences.n: «auſſi … que» is ‘as … as’. «fit loger» ‘made lodge’ is «faire» with an infinitive, ‘had lodged’. «marier» with an object is ‘to give in marriage, to marry off’: Cendrillon arranges the matches. «dés le jour même» (modern «dès le jour même») is ‘that very same day’, and «grands Seigneurs» were great nobles.

sentences.t: MORALITE
sentences.say: MORALITÉ
sentences.l: MORAL
sentences.n: «MORALITE» is ‘moral’, printed without the accent of «moralité». The verses belong to the tale as the book prints it, and this tale has two morals, the second headed «AUTRE MORALITÉ».

«le ſexe» on its own meant ‘women, the fair sex’ in the French of the time; the literal line keeps ‘the sex’, and the idiomatic line says ‘women’. «De l’admirer jamais on ne ſe laſſe» ‘of admiring it never does one tire’ puts «jamais» ‘never’ early for the verse, and «ſe laſſer de» is ‘to tire of’. «bonne grace» (modern «bonne grâce») is graciousness, the charm of a pleasing manner, and the whole moral turns on it. «treſor» is «trésor», «encor» is a spelling of «encore» ‘still’ that verse used to save a syllable, and «ſans prix» is ‘beyond price’.

sentences.t:
C’eſt ce qu’à Cendrillon fit avoir ſa Maraine,
En la dreſſant, en l’inſtruiſant,
Tant & ſi bien qu’elle en fit une Reine :
(Car ainſi ſur ce conte on va moraliſant.)
sentences.say:
C’est ce qu’à Cendrillon fit avoir sa Marraine,
En la dressant, en l’instruisant,
Tant et si bien qu’elle en fit une Reine :
(Car ainsi sur ce conte on va moralisant.)
sentences.l:
It is this that her godmother made Cendrillon have,
In training her, in instructing her,
So much and so well that she made of her a Queen:
(For thus upon this tale one goes moralising.)
sentences.i:
That is what her godmother gave Cinderella,
by forming her and instructing her,
to such good purpose that she made her a queen
(for this is how one draws a moral from this tale).
sentences.n: «C’eſt ce qu’à Cendrillon fit avoir ſa Maraine» turns the French order about for the rhyme, with «ſa Maraine» the subject at the end of the line; «faire avoir» is ‘to get (someone) something’, and «ce» ‘this’ is the «bonne grace» of the verse before. «dreſſer» is ‘to train, to form’ and «inſtruire» ‘to instruct, to bring up’: the moral credits the godmother with the girl’s manners, which the tale itself never shows her teaching. «tant & ſi bien que» is ‘so much and so well that’, and «en fit une Reine» ‘made a queen of her’ gives the Prince’s bride her future title. «on va moraliſant» ‘one goes moralising’ is «aller» with a present participle, ‘one goes on moralising’, and the bracketed aside smiles at the business of drawing morals.

sentences.t:
Belles, ce don vaut mieux que d’eſtre bien coëffées,
Pour engager un cœur, pour en venir à bout,
La bonne grace eſt le vrai don des Fées ;
Sans elle on ne peut rien, avec elle on peut tout.
sentences.say:
Belles, ce don vaut mieux que d’être bien coiffées,
Pour engager un cœur, pour en venir à bout,
La bonne grâce est le vrai don des Fées ;
Sans elle on ne peut rien, avec elle on peut tout.
sentences.l:
Beauties, this gift is worth more than to be well coiffed,
To engage a heart, to come to the end of it,
Good grace is the true gift of the fairies;
Without it one can do nothing, with it one can do all.
sentences.n: «Belles» ‘beauties’ is the moral’s address to its women readers. «bien coëffées» ‘well coiffed’ recalls the sisters’ headdresses and the hours Cendrillon spent on their hair. «engager un cœur» is ‘to win a heart, to bind its affection’, and «en venir à bout» ‘to come to the end of it’, ‘to succeed’, is the phrase the tale used of the sisters who could not get their feet into the slipper. «le vrai don des Fées» is ‘the true gift of the fairies’, set above the fairy gifts of the tales. The witness ends the first line with a comma where English wants a stronger stop, and the idiomatic line uses a semicolon.

sentences.t: AUTRE MORALITÉ
sentences.l: ANOTHER MORAL

sentences.t:
C’eſt ſans doute un grand avantage
D’avoir de l’eſprit, du courage,
De la naiſſance, du bon ſens,
Et d’autres ſemblables talens
Qu’on reçoit du Ciel en partage ;
sentences.say:
C’est sans doute un grand avantage,
D’avoir de l’esprit, du courage,
De la naissance, du bon sens,
Et d’autres semblables talents,
Qu’on reçoit du Ciel en partage ;
sentences.l:
It is without doubt a great advantage
To have wit, courage,
Birth, good sense,
And other like talents
That one receives from Heaven as a share;
sentences.i:
It is certainly a great advantage
to have courage and wit,
good birth and good sense,
and other such gifts
as Heaven deals out to us;
sentences.n: «ſans doute» meant ‘without doubt, certainly’ in 1697; modern French has softened it to ‘probably’. «eſprit» is ‘wit’, a quick and graceful mind, rather than ‘spirit’. «naiſſance» ‘birth’ is good birth, a noble family. «talens» is «talents», the 1697 plural without its t. «recevoir en partage» is ‘to receive as one’s portion’, the share of gifts Heaven hands to each.

sentences.t:
Mais vous aurez beau les avoir,
Pour voſtre avancement ce ſeront choſes vaines
Si vous n’avez, pour les faire valoir,
Ou des parrains, ou des Maraines.
sentences.say:
Mais vous aurez beau les avoir,
Pour votre avancement ce seront choses vaines,
Si vous n’avez, pour les faire valoir,
Ou des parrains, ou des Marraines.
sentences.l:
But you will have them in vain,
For your advancement these will be vain things
If you have not, to make them count,
Either godfathers, or godmothers.
sentences.i:
but have them as you may,
they will do nothing to advance you
unless you have, to make the most of them,
godfathers or godmothers.
sentences.n: «vous aurez beau les avoir» ‘you will have them in vain’: «avoir beau» with an infinitive is to do something to no purpose. «avancement» is getting on in the world, at court or in office. «faire valoir» is ‘to make (something) count, to show it to advantage’. «parrains» and «Maraines» are godfathers and godmothers, and here also patrons, the well-placed friends who push a career forward: the second moral stands the first on its head, crediting the godmother’s influence rather than the girl’s grace. «voſtre» is «votre», and «ce ſeront» ‘these will be’ is the future.
